subtopic: PRESENTATION TO CANADA BT GOVERNMENTS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM, AUSTRALIA AND NEW' ZEALAND

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRESENTATION TO CANADA BT GOVERNMENTS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM, AUSTRALIA AND NEW' ZEALAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the close of last year I received a letter signed by the high commissioners in Canada for the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, informing me that the governments of their respective countries jointly desired, as a permanent memorial of the British commonwealth air training plan, to present a gift of wrought iron gates for the entrance to the air station at Trenton, Ontario. Attached to the letter was a preliminary sketch of the proposed memorial gates.
An earlier proposal was an avenue of English oak trees terminated at either end by pavilions of native timbers from Australia and New Zealand. In due course the oak trees wTere planted. On reconsideration it was felt that, due to impermanence, wooden pavilions would not be entirely suitable. The governments of the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand accordingly decided that wrought iron gates for the entrance to the air station, where they would be in line with the oak trees already growing there, would be a more suitable gift.
It is with warm appreciation of its value and significance that the government of Canada, on behalf of the Canadian people, has accepted this memorial gift. We in Canada, in common with free peoples the world over, will ever remember the contribution to victory which resulted from the British commonwealth air training plan. The young men of the nations of the commonwealth who trained in Canada will long be gratefully remembered. Their residence in our homeland served to strengthen the bonds of kinship which unite the peoples of our respective countries. These beautiful gates will serve not only as a memorial of efforts made in the common cause, but as an enduring symbol of the unity of the peoples of the British commonwealth.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESIGNATIONS AND OTHER CHANGES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESIGNATIONS AND OTHER CHANGES
speechtext:
As hon. members are aware, on January 19 the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Right Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, resigned. Mr. Mackenzie was later appointed to the senate. I hold in my hand copies of the letters which were exchanged between Mr. Mackenzie and myself. I could read them to the house, but perhaps hon. members would give their consent to have them appear in Hansard.
(The correspondence follows):
Canada
Minister of Veterans Affairs
Ottawa, January 15, 1918.
My dear Prime Minister:-
At various times during the last two years I brought to your attention medical certificates indicating that my health was somewhat impaired. Although the condition is now greatly improved, I feel it my duty to separate myself, for the time being, at least, from administrative duties.
Therefore, now, before the session resumes, I, with deep regret, submit my resignation from your able administration.
May I take this opportunity of tendering to you. sir, my very deep appreciation for many kindnesses and much encouragement during the time I served with you. and also to ask you to thank my colleagues for unfailing courtesy in our united service to our country.
I am proud to say that the Department of Veterans Affairs, over which I have presided for eight years, is in an excellent state of efficient organization. It has rendered and is rendering noble service to those who served and saved Canada in the dark days.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) Ian A. Mackenzie The Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, January 16, 1948.
The Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, P.C., M.P., Minister of Veterans Affairs,
Ottawa.
My dear Mackenzie:
I have received your letter of yesterday, in which, because of impaired health, you ask to be relieved of your present administrative duties as Minister of Veterans Affairs over which department you have presided since its inception.	_
In the light of the circumstances you mention, I feel I have no alternative but to submit your resignation to the Governor General and to
[Mr. Mackenzie King.)
advise His Excellency's acceptance of it. Before, however, submitting your resignation to His Excellency, may I say how greatly I regret the circumstances which render that step advisable, and how sincerely I trust that freedom from the responsibilities of office will afford just what is required to effect a further restoration of your health and strength.
May I also say how very much I shall miss the close association we have enjoyed over many years in the cabinet, and your helpful co-operation in the work of the administration. I know these feelings will be shared by all our colleagues.
While I realize that freedom from administrative duties will afford opportunity for further improvement in your health. I should be sorry ' if the severance of your relations with the Department of Veterans Affairs were to mean that parliament, at any future time, would lose the benefit of your knowledge and understanding of the problems of Canada's veterans, and of your wide and long experience in public affairs.
To ensure your continued membership in the parliament of Canada, I should, with the consent of our colleagues, be prepared to recommend to His Excellency your immediate appointment to the Senate of Canada, to fill one of the vacancies at present existing in the representation of British Columbia in the upper house.
As appointment to the Senate would involve your giving up your seat in the House of Commons, I should be grateful if, before I speak of the matter in council, you would let me know of your willingness to accept an appointment to the Senate, should the appointment be recommended by the cabinet and approved by His Excellency.
With kindest personal regards,
Yours very sincerely',
(Sgd.) W. h. Mackenzie King.
On the resignation of the Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, as Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Hon. Milton Gregg, who had been Minister of Fisheries, was appointed to the portfolio of Veterans Affairs. He resigned the portfolio of Fisheries. The Hon. James A. MacKinnon was appointed Minister of Fisheries and resigned as Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Right Hon. Clarence Howe was appointed Minister of Trade and Commerce. Mr. Howe will continue to hold the portfolio of Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, which he has held for some time past. The affairs of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply are being gradually wound up. The work of the Department of National War Services has 'been completed. The department itself having ceased to exist, Hon. James J. McCann's resignation as minister of that department has been accepted.
I desire to table the orders in council with respect to the portfolios I have mentioned. They include the appointment of Mr. Howe as Minister of Trade and Commerce, of Mr. MacKinnon as Minister of Fisheries, and Mr. Gregg as Minister of Veterans Affairs, and

Business of the House
the acceptance of the resignation of Mr. McCann as Minister of National War Services.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS ON WEDNESDAYS AND THURSDAYS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS ON WEDNESDAYS AND THURSDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I now
say a word to the house about the business, as the government has thought it can most effectively be carried on at this time.
When the house met in December last the proceedings of the house were governed by the following motion;
That the debate on the address in reply to the speech of His Excellency the Governor General to both houses of parliament be the first order of business on Monday December 8th instant, and that this order be followed by government notices of motion and government orders notwithstanding anything in standing order 15.
That motion was agreed to on December 8. At the time it was agreed .to I stated it was not the government's intention to have the motion stand indefinitely, but that it would remain at least until the end of that part of the session which was being held before Christmas, or if sittings had continued after Christmas it would stand until the old year was out.
No question was asked at the conclusion of sitting on the last day the house sat before the Christmas adjournment as to what business would be proceeded with today. If there had been, it would have been mentioned at the time that we would continue with the debate on the exchange conservation measure, which was before the house at the time. There having been no formal statement in the house to that effect, I asked my secretary at the end of last week to see that the leaders of the different parties were informed that this would be the first order of business today.
The government has had under consideration the very point my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has brought up, namely the question of how long we should postpone further debate on the address. Hon. members well know that the emergency measures, so named, are important measures, and should be proceeded with as soon as possible. However we have felt that hon. members would undoubtedly wish to get under way with the debate on the address, so as not to be deprived of opportunities thus afforded.
We have thought that probably the whole situation could be best met if for two days in the week we were to take up the debate on the address, and for three days we were to discuss the emergency measures. So far as the government is concerned this would have the advantage of allowing the Minister of Finance a little more time for the preparation of further measures he will have to bring on later. Also in .this way the minister would not have to be in the house continuously throughout the week in connection noth the emergency measures. The time given over to debate on the address would permit of his having some opportunity to consider other matters.
Business oj the House

Except to the extent I have just indicated, we have felt that the emergency measures should have precedence over any others. In this connection there will be, of course, later on the transitional powers bill, one similar to the one passed at the last session of palia-ment. It would be in the same form, but not as lengthy. If the orders in council appended to this bill are to be continued in force, that measure of necessity would have to pass before the end of the present fiscal year.
I might say at once that I am quite open to receive comment from hon. members opposite with respect to this suggested program. If there is any real disagreement between us we can consider what other steps might be preferable or advisable. I hope, however, that upon reflection hon. members will see that in the end we shall probably make more progress with these emergency measures and the debate on the address if they are carried on more or less simultaneously during this part of the session.
The proposal, then, w'ould be to proceed in that order, giving priority to government business until the exchange conservation measures and the transitional powers bill are disposed of. The exchange conservation measures would include items numbers 4 and 5 on today's order paper, the tax resolutions already introduced, and the bills to be based upon them. The transitional powers bill, as I have said, will be in a form similar to that of last year, but the schedule will be shorter.
Of course all this is subject to the proposal that we reserve two days each week- and I am suggesting that they be Wednesday and Thursday-for the debate on the address. The government would wish to reserve its right to bring in any special measure or any important measure which might have to be dealt with within a certain time. At this moment I am not aware of anything except one bill that relates to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This would have to be dealt with before February 15 because of a time limit fixed by the existing legislation.
Motions to set up standing and special committees of the house will be taken up from time to time as circumstances warrant. Once the speech from the throne and the other measures I have mentioned have been disposed of, the government proposes then to proceed with the resolution respecting the Geneva agreements and other government business.
It might help to regularize the discussion were I now to present to the house the motion that I had in mind in regard to

taking two days a week for the debate on the address, and I would therefore move, seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley):
That the order for the consideration of the motion for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session be considered on Wednesdays and Thursdays until disposed of and notwithstanding the resolution passed by the house on December 8, 1947.

speechtext:
The point I was concerned with when I rose to speak was as to when the house would have an opportunity of discussing the question which most of us think is the urgent question before the people of this country, namely, the rapid rise in the cost of living. When I saw that the debate on the address was postponed, and not knowing what the government's policy was going to be, and when we had no indication as to when the parliamentary committee proposed by the Prime Minister a few days ago would be set up, I intended to move the adjournment of the house to discuss the particular matter of the high cost of living. We feel that however important the exchange conservation program of the government may be, however important the transitional powers measure may be. the rise in the cost of living far transcends them in importance.
The Prime Minister has brought forward a motion under which two days out of the

Business of the House
five will be given to a discussion of the speech from the throne, when private members can bring forward their grievances or other suggestions. In so far as that program is concerned I have no objection. I think it is quite reasonable. But I should like to ask the Prime 'Minister when he intends to bring forward the motion to set up a parliamentary committee to deal with price spreads. We feel that that policy is not adequate, that it is simply an effort to shift responsibility from the government to this house and1 to postpone unnecessarily the consideration of high living costs. We know from the experience we have had in connection with the work of previous parliamentary committees just what it will mean. We do not think that plan is adequate.
So far as the general program, aside from the particular issue of the cost of living, is concerned, we on this side will accept the Prime Minister's motion. I should like to ask him to indicate how soon the motion on price spreads will be brought forward. We think it ought to be discussed at the earliest possible time-and we mean early. If we could have such an assurance, then I would not proceed with this motion today. But in view of the importance of this matter, in view of the different lines of attack which different parties are advancing I thing it is in the interests of the public that that one issue should be aired in order that all may understand the situation and the best ways of arriving at a solution.
In conclusion may I say that I accept the Prime Minister's suggested program, namely, two days in the week for the speech from the throne and three days for government business, but I should like his assurance that the motion to set up a committee to deal with the rise in the cost of living will be brought forward early. I suggest that it be almost immediately. I do not think that is an unreasonable request to make of the Prime Minister. If he will accept that, then I would not go forward today with this motion, but otherwise I would feel it necessary to do so.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS ON WEDNESDAYS AND THURSDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the two weeks session before Christmas the house agreed to defer discussion on the address. We were agreeable because we felt that the increase in the cost of living and the extension of controls was the principal business before the house. We made our position clear at that time. I am disappointed that the Prime Minister has made the suggestion he has. I believe that the mixing up of two or three debates in this house is not good business, either for the
house or for any one of the debates. What we should do is to carry on and complete one debate before we initiate another.
The debate on the address is looked upon by hon. members, particularly those who do not have the chance of speaking as much as some of the rest of us, as an opportunity to air the grievances of their constituents and to discuss general problems affecting domestic and even international relations. I am sorry that the leader of the opposition has agreed to the program suggested by the Prime Minister. From what he said I gathered that the Prime Minister was quite willing to hear suggestions from this side of the house and was not going to press unnecessarily the program placed before the house.
I think I speak for those who sit around me, although I have had no opportunity of discussing the matter with them. I might say that I was not in my office on Saturday and did not know of the telephone call until it was too late to do anything about it. I want to make it quite clear that as far as we are concerned we think we should proceed immediately with the debate on the address, conclude that debate and then go on to the other matters that are before us. We would have agreed gladly to an interruption in the debate on the address in order to set up any committees or to deal with the one farm problem the Prime Minister mentioned, but I certainly think that both the country and the house expect that an opportunity will be given to hon. members to go on with the debate on the address, and, having concluded that, to take up the other matters outlined in the suggested program placed before us by the Prime Minister.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, this group would like to take a similar position to that taken by the leader of the C.C.F. party. We have constantly held that the most important business before this house until it is disposed of is the debate on the address, and we feel that there is a likelihood of considerable useless repetition if one debate is not disposed of before another is initiated. I think further that the Prime Minister could have helped the situation considerably if he had called in the leaders of the parties to discuss what might be an acceptable program for at least the first two weeks after the resumption of the session, and I am hoping that he will yet see fit to do that. Inevitably it would lead to better co-operation, as the experience of past sessions shows.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS ON WEDNESDAYS AND THURSDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear from what the leader of the opposition has said that he and I have had the same thought in our minds; indeed, it is the
Business oj the House

thought of all who have spoken, namely, that it would be the wish of hon. members to have the debate on the address proceeded with fairly soon, if not immediately. I would point out however that there is no limit of time to the debate on the address. If the debate were to be limited to a fe\v days or to a week or two, if hon. gentlemen would be prepared to limit it to a comparatively short time, the government would be quite prepared to give at once the entire right of way to the debate on the address. On the other hand, without any such limitation, the debate on the address, once it starts, might go on for two or three or four weeks. No one can say how long it would last, as past experience shows.
On the other hand we have certain measures that are extremely important. Taxes are being collected under legislation that is before the house, and imports are being restricted. We do not wish as a government to continue doing that unless we have the support of this house, and we want to get that support just as soon as we possibly can or know if it is not to be given. That is the reason why we wish to proceed without any more delay than is possible to having the emergency measures passed by the two houses of parliament if they are to be sanctioned at all.
The leader of the opposition has made a suggestion which I think will help to meet what the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Social Credit party have in mind. Evidently we all feel that the cost of living is one question that is uppermost in the minds of the people of this country. Certainly it is, and the purpose of the government in proposing a committee of this house to investigate matters pertaining thereto is evidence of the fact that we have felt very strongly that that matter should receive the fullest investigation possible. That 'being so, may I say to my hon. friend that I can see no reason why that committee might not be appointed within a fortnight. If in his opinion that is too long a time, I will make it a week.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I rose a few minutes ago it was for the purpose of endeavouring to have the government bring forward the debate on the cost of living situation in Canada, and to have it dealt with immediately or as early as possible. The Prime Minister has now indicated that the earliest he feels he can bring it forward is in a week or so. My desire was not expressed with the view of having the parliamentary committee set up in a hurry. I do not think that is going to solve this problem. My desire was to have this issue considered by all parties advancing their views and the government stating its position, because I think that is what the Canadian people are waiting for. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if that can be done the debate on the speech from the throne will be cut at least in half and the house will save a great deal of time. I think that is the issue that the people, and if I may say so, the members of this house, want to deal with perhaps more than all other issues put together. In view of the situation which confronts us, it will now drag on in the debate on the speech from the throne and will be only one of many other matters to be dealt with. Because of that I feel that I should advance my motion. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell) the adjournment of the house under standing order 31, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the sudden and unprecedented rise in the cost of living.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has just moved a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. Hon. members know that it is the practice to move such a motion to give an opportunity to hon. members to ventilate any grievances which they might have. In the debate on the motion put forward by the Prime Minister a few moments ago it was mentioned that hon. members will have an opportunity on Wednesday and Thursday to take part in the debate on the speech from the throne. During that time hon. members will have the opportunity to discuss the question. mentioned by the leader of the opposition, namely, the rising cost of living. Therefore the hon. member will have an opportunity to discuss that matter not tomorrow but the day after tomorrow. Because of that
I do not think we should adjourn the house to discuss a matter which the house will have an opportunity to discuss two days from now, particularly when we have urgent matters before us. Therefore I do not see any urgency in the motion of the leader of the opposition, and I cannot receive it.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: May I be permitted to make one observation, Mr. Speaker? I quite realize that in your capacity as Speaker you have the right to decide in your judgment whether a matter is urgent or not. We recognize that right, and no one desires t.o take * it from you. None the less, some of us disagree with you. I could protest your decision, but I know your decision would then be that we have no right to protest the decision. I could then protest your right to say that we have no right to protest your decision. If that came to a vote the majority sitting to your right would support you. In such circumstances I do not propose to waste the time of the house by going through all these motions. I just wish to observe that as much as we respect you and your judgment, we disagree with you in the position you take.

subtopic: MOTION FOB ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I believe it is my duty to call the attention of the house to the fact that when the Speaker decides to refuse a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of public importance it is not because the Speaker believes that a matter which an hon. member would like to have discussed in the house is not urgent and is not important. The question that the Speaker has to decide is whether the matter is urgent and important and the house has no other opportunity to discuss it because there is nothing on the order paper to permit the discussion. If hon. members have no other opportunity according to the order paper to discuss the matter, the Speaker may permit a motion to adjourn the house to give hon. members an opportunity to air their grievances, but when on the order paper there is an item in the discussion of which hon. members have the opportunity to air their grievances, the Speaker has no alternative but to refuse to accept the motion to adjourn the house, since it is not urgent.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, December 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): The more highly developed a country's economy becomes, the more likely it is that there will be interruptions in the steadiness of that economy, and the question therefore arises whether or not the interruptions that occur are more easily ironed out by the natural working of economic laws or by the interposition of governmental controls. In this connection I am reminded of the statement of an astute professor of Harvard university who once said:
Bight three times out of five: success. Wrong three times out of five: the sheriff.
We do not expect the Minister of Finance or his advisers to be always right in financial matters, but I think it will be conceded by all except the government itself that the decision taken on July 5, 1946, to revalue the

Foreign Exchange Conservation
Canadian dollar from 90 cents to 100 cents United States was a mistaken decision. It has been termed by some the greatest administrative error in the history of Canada.
It is impossible for the government to be always right in its economic guesses as to the future. It is infinitely sounder to allow as much freedom as possible to the natural working of economic forces. In 1946 the government relied on three different things taking place, none of which happened. In the first place the government thought international trade would expand, and that with the expansion we should have greater convertibility of sterling into dollars. In the second place the government thought that with the doing away of price controls in the United States on July l, prices in that country first of all would go up rapidly and later-and shortly-they would come down. Again they were wrong. In the third place the government thought the greatly expanded imports from the United States into Canada would level off. The fact is that since that time they have continued to increase at an accelerated rate. Still we find that even though the three main reasons, perhaps, on which the government relied, all turned out to be wrong guesses, the government still believes it took the right decision on July 5, 1946. They are very much like the popular version of King Canute endeavouring to withstand the economic tides. It is impossible for this or any other government to withstand the economic tides with which it meets, especially if it guesses wrongly. If ever there was a time for confession and repentance it is now, before the monkey-wrenches which by the bill now before us the government has thrown into the machinery of Canadian business have set in motion a depression from which the recovery may be very painful.
There is no certainty in finance. An operation upon the economic body is much more difficult than one upon the human body. Just as doctors, despite their hundreds of thousands and the millions of dollars spent on medical research, cannot cure us of a common cold, so economic doctors, backed by the supreme power of the state, cannot cure even simple maladjustments in our economy. Occasionally an economist like John Maynard Keynes, who was a great economic diagnostician, comes to the fore; but in his last contribution even he turned toward the natural working of economic forces and away from state-induced reactions. In the human field one body is physically very much like another, but there is only one economic body and that is largely unpredictable because it is governed by the hopes and fears of the peoples of the world. Fortunately the natural workings of these hopes and fears, these

ambitions and cautions, by observation have been reduced to economic laws from which there is no escape so long as human nature remains what it is. Regulations, except where they ease stricter regulations, are hindrances to the production and exchange of goods and services. One regulation breeds another. The present quotas, embargoes and excise taxes all flow from the hurried and disastrous decision made on July 5, 1946, when our dollar was given the same value as the United States dollar. There is no particular reason, Mr. Speaker, why Canadian beavers should sell for the same as American eagles.
Time may not permit me to recount the disastrous effects of the present regulations on some trades, and on employment; but we find that even the Department of Labour, in accounting for the increased unemployment in certain parts of the country, ascribes some of it to the workings of the present exchange regulations. Some businesses have been forced to close. Many of these were newly established importing and distributing firms which had been so hopefully set up by young veterans. Other businesses have been compelled to reduce staffs and further reductions in staff are forthcoming. The pity of it is that no one knows how long these iniquitous regulations and controls will last, and employers know not whether to disband their organizations or to look upon the present calamitous restrictions as temporary and keep their organizations intact. The great buying public have found that the restrictions have resulted in the greatest and fastest increase in the cost of living in our history. For this the Liberal government is solely and directly to blame.
On July 5, 1946, our exchange and price situation with the United States had found a reasonable balance, with a net inflow of United States funds into Canada. Due to an administrative error the $1,500 million of United States reserves which Canada then had now have dwindled to a few hundred million dollars. Had our dollar remained at 90 cents United States, or been allowed to follow its natural course, we would not have been forced to accept a European diet, or forced to accept a state of national beggary; nor would we have caused consternation to many of our business people, bringing grievous hardship to many who were formerly employed and forcing up the cost of living to all.
In order to continue the administrative error and to permit the government, ostrichlike, to claim that it was right on July 5, 1946, we have been forced to go hat in hand to the United States to borrow American dollars, so that we may not further reduce employment and the standard of living of our people. We

________________Foreign Exchange Conservation
have borrowed $300,000,000 from the United States export-import bank to tide us over the next few months until some fairy godmother, such as the Marshall plan, comes to our rescue. We may hope for the best, but we are leaning on a very uncertain support.
Uet us examine what the asking of this $300,000,000 loan involves. It is well known that Canada endeavoured to raise funds from private American sources, but in the unprejudiced eyes of our American friends we were regarded as a profligate country which had no visible means of repaying any sizeable loan we might make in the United States. It would be interesting to the house to learn how much or how little was offered to our great country by these unprejudiced lenders of American private capital, and for how long the loan was to be and what were the terms. Did our government try the great American insurance companies, and what terms did they offer?
Let us look at Canada's dollar position through the eyes of an unprejudiced outsider. In 1946 we had United States reserves of $1,500 million, largely the result not of trading but of the sale of American investments formerly held by Canadians, and of the dollar proceeds of American investment in Canada. This $1,500 million has been largely frittered aw'ay by our government as a result of its decision of July 5, 1946; and the frittering continued on an increasing scale, until the fatal day could be postponed no longer. When I spoke on this matter in December, three per cent Canadian bonds were selling in Canada at 104. The same bonds were freely traded by the large institutions in New York at 87, a difference of 17 points, which was a fair measure of the value the Americans put on the Canadian dollar at that time; and there has been no significant change since. How could it be apparent to a lender in the United States that Canada could repay any American borrowing? We had made it more difficult for our industries to export to the United States; we had cut our gold mining industry in two, and so far as United States imports were concerned we were living very much like drunken sailors. Canada was denied the private channels of borrowing in the United States and in view of our monthly deficits on exchange account was compelled to turn to a United States government agency, the export-import bank, for a loan of $300 million.
Let us examine what this export-import bank is. It was set up in 1934, and I quote-
To aid in financing and to facilitate exports and imports and the exchange of commodities between the United States or any of its territories, or insular possessions and any foreign country or the agencies or nationals thereof.
5849-35i
Its capital was set at a billion dollars, and its total loans may not exceed $3.5 billions. It makes loans only for specific purposes. They do not give to Canada $300 million to do with what she thinks is in her best interests. She must set forth exactly the purposes and requirements she has in mind, and we can do with the money only that which the bank considers proper. Surely that is an unbecoming position for a great country like Canada to find itself in! The bank makes only those loans which offer a reasonable assurance of repayment. Thus it is prepared to take greater chances than private bankers feel justified in taking with their customers' savings.
May I quote further from the rules governing the export-import bank:
In accordance with the policy laid down by congress the bank does not compete with private capital, but rather supplements and encourages it. The activities of the bank are confined, therefore, to dealing with risks of the type described in this statement, which are either beyond the scope of private capital or which private capital is not prepared to assume without government assistance.
Will anyone say that the Canadian loan is beyond the scope of private capital in the United States?-because for decades the United States market has been even greedy of Canadian loans, our record for repayment and for the handling of our own domestic economy has been so sound. We find today, however, that a loan to Canada from private sources in the United States is apparently beyond the scope of private capital. One other point which is mentioned in the rule governing the bank is that the loan shall be one which private capital would not accept without government assistance. Here not only is there government assistance by way of guarantee, but it is a direct obligation of the Canadian government. Yet there are not private takers for a Canadian loan in the United States, if that loan is repayable in American dollars. It is indeed a sorry plight in which this government has placed the finances and credit of this great country.
Over and over again in the handbook published by the United States government describing the activities of the export-import bank we find it expressly stated that the bank shall not compete with private capital. For example, here is a quotation:
The bank is expressly prohibited from competing with private capital and does not, therefore, extend credits when private credit is available in adequate amounts on reasonable terms.
I think possibly the Minister of Finance, or whoever went down for the government to the United States to endeavour to raise an

Foreign Exchange Conservation
American loan, found that the amounts offered were most inadequate. I should say that the $300 million loan is inadequate, when we have lost about 81,000 million in American credits *during the last twelve months.
When the application for a loan is made to *the export-import bank there must be shown:
O) Justification for seeking the assistance of the export-import bank, including satisfactory evidence that private credit is not available.
(2)	A statement of external assets of the country in the form of gold and foreign exchange, showing official holdings, separately from private holdings and holdings ot dollars separately from holdings of other currencies.
(3)	Current and prospective rate of gold production.
I am sure we shall have a sorry picture .when we have to reveal that, our gold production being more than cut in two, as a 'direct reflection upon our credit and upon our borrowing power in the United States and elsewhere. Then, further, there must be shown:
\ statement of the international investment position of the country at long-term and sliort-. term, including major commitments, pending or . contemplated, and an estimate of the amounts of interest and amortization due annually over the life of the loan on external fixed-service obligations, together with a statement of priorities, if any, in loan service.
Once upon, a time before this government took unto itself the tampering with exchange, and before eliminating any regard for the natural working of exchange forces, there was in Canada a considerable investment in * American securities. Those investments were sold partly in the early days of the war to help finance our early obligations before the entry of the United States; and that reserve has been very sadly depleted, so that today it is but a fraction of what it once was. Under the rules of the foreign exchange control board there is no possibility of increasing or augmenting that reserve; so should there come a more vital necessity we would have a substantially .smaller amount of American investments privately held in Canada. We have been living on our capital. Here the requirement is that an analysis of the country's ability to repay on the basis of its current and prospective balance of payments must be shown.
I am sure that if I were a lender in the United States and I had in trust certain sums at my disposal, and if I were to take a look at the record of Canada under the present government and were to see how it has frittered away the $1,500 million of United States credits which it had, and note that $1,000 million of it had gone in one year, it would certainly say that that country was

not a fit one to receive a loan, because it had no apparent means of repaying it. That must be obvious to anyone.
A review of the letters and documents with regard to Canada's attempt to borrow in the United States would be most revealing, and the production of these papers will be asked for. In fact it would not be surprising to see the administration of the export-import bank in the United States questioned on the floor of the United States Congress.
I just wish to quote from a letter from the acting manager of the export-import bank to our own Minister of Finance in connection with this $300 million loan. Th. acting manager, Mr. Herbert Gaston says this:
We note that the Canadian government believes that it would be desirable to reduce the commitment of the export-import bank and that it intends in the near future to approach the private capital market in the United States for credit facilities with this end in view.
Of course it must be known to all that the government has already applied to the private market in the United States, and did not receive a satisfactory response. I was amused at the minister's statement when the loan was announced. This report says:
Finance Minister Abbott said it was planned to seek a reduction of the bank's commitment by sale of Canadian securities in this market-
That is the United States market.
-if and when the capacity of the investment market had been determined.
The capacity of the United States investment market for 8300 million or $500 million!

speechtext:
If the minister says that he did not say it, I will retract it. I would like to point out that the capacity of the United States market for any amount that Canada might want is almost limitless. Private corporations like the American Telephone and Telegraph Company can borrow to one billion dollars and oil companies can borrow $300 million or $500 million apparently without any difficulty. I suppose in a month there must be many occasions on which private
54a

Foreign Exchange Conservation
industry would borrow more than the small requirements of Canada. To quote again the acting manager of the bank:
We note that the Canadian government believes that it would be desirable to reduce the commitment of the export-import bank and that it intends in the near future to approach the private capital market in the United States for credit facilities with this end in view. That this should be done at as early a date as possible is a matter of primary concern to the bank because of its statutory responsibility not to compete with but rather* to encourage and supplement the use of private capital in financing United States foreign trade.
What I suggest is that the manager of the bank knew very well that he was on rather thin ice when he made this loan to Canada because our country would not meet the terms of private capital or would not so put its house in order that it was a fit subject for a loan from private resources in the United States.
Thus we see the path down which the Liberal administration has led the credit of this country. In regard to United States borrowings, we are virtually in the position of a bankrupt country. The revaluation of our dollar to 100 cents United States has brought about this unenviable condition. The drastic restrictions embodied in the legislation now before us are a last-minute attempt to avert national insolvency. Unfortunately they are like insulin; they merely keep the patient alive from day to day and cure nothing. On the other hand, a recognition of its administrative errors by our government and the restoration of our dollar to 90 cents United States-all within the terms of Bretton Woods -and to lower than 90 cents if conditions necessitate it-will bring about a natural correction and set in motion those economic forces which will permanently cure any deficit in our business relations with the United States and cause the least disruption to the business and employment of our people.
We shall not then have a set of slapdash regulations throttling Canadian enterprise slapped on without a moment's thought, regulations in which there have already been a thousand modifications. And now the import regulations on iron and steel machinery and structural steel have been postponed "until further notice". Business must plan not only for tomorrow but for years ahead. Unless we follow a sound currency policy and restore freedom to our businessmen we are heading for a false and unnatural economy and unemployment and depression for our people. The only hope for the prosperity of our people lies in the policy of the Progressive Conservative party.

Mr; Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on Bill No. 3, respecting measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources. I should like to refer for a moment to my genial friend, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman). The best rebuttal of. the speech which he commenced last year and ended at 4.30 this afternoon-
That was not his fault.

I am willing to concede that 

wherein he claimed that private enterprise, his enterprise, could rectify the excessive spending of the Canadian government in the United States is to attempt to show the h-on. gentleman the error of his own thinking. During the whole period of time during which we have had trade relations with our neighbour to the south the only time that we had a credit balance, if that is desirable, the only time that we had a surplus of United States dollars was during the period of world war II when the Canadian government adopted some form of planning of our foreign exchange resources.	_
Last December 16 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) explained this bill by saying that it would be one prong of a three-pronged fork, so -to speak, which his government considered it desirable to use in order to meet Canada's perennial shortage of United States dollars. This the government seeks to do by the bill now before us. The other two were, first a subsidy to be paid to Canada's goldmining industry, and, second, a further huge excise tax of 25 per cent or more to be added to the excise and sales taxes already provided for by our statute books and imposed on a wide variety of consumer goods in Canada.
The minister indicated that except for the very few years of the war we have always bought more United States goods than we have sold in that country. This has always left us short of United States money, the hard cash with which to balance our trade with that country. We got around the shortage of United States money in various ways. We borrowed United States money, and we dug gold from the Canadian mines and buried it in a mine in Kentucky. Then we adopted the practice of using credit balances that we had accumulated by selling more goods to Great Britain and Europe than we bought in return, which balances have until very recently been convertible into hard cash or United States currency, by which we settled our debit balances with the United States.
The Minister of Finance hopes to cure this imbalance with Bill No. 3, which is one-third of his operations. I think it will be

Foreign Exchange Conservation
ineffective, and that not all of his proposed cure is necessary. When to the weaknesses of Bill No. 3 you add the injustice of the 25 per cent excise tax superimposed) on the various sales taxes, and with decontrol now in effect, you are cutting the financial props from under a considerable number of people in this country who rely on appropriate trade and monetary policies for their well-being-the wage earner, the man on fixed income, and so on.
The Minister of Finance has guaranteed an inflationary situation which will take the cost of living several points higher than it is at present. The minister prophesied that this measure would1 be of short-term duration to meet an abnormal situation. But what was abnormal yesterdlay might be considered quite normal tomorrow, and we may have a continuation of the terms of this bill indefinitely.
I think, too, it is childish to argue that if Canada must buy less from the United States to rectify our dollar shortage we must therefore also buy less from Great Britain and other countries of Europe with which we have not now a trading deficit but to which we have been selling considerably more than we have been buying back in return. The minister in effect says that while we wish to continue selling to these countries, nevertheless we must buy still less from them in return. We have always bought less from Britain than we have exported to her. Why restrict our purchases from her still more, as wiil be done under schedule I of Bill 3, which debars imports from Great Britain or any other country equally with imports from the United States, whose currency we lack. How can we stabilize our food sales to the United Kingdom if we shut the dloor on British manufactured goods in return? Sometimes when we read of the secret negotiations that go on from time to time between ambassadors of various countries I wonder whether the Canadian government has made secret trade commitments which will have the effect of reducing our imports from the United Kingdom. If so, to whom have these commitments been made, and why have they been ipadle?
We have not yet approved the Geneva trade agreement. But if we do approve that agreement, its terms permit us to shut off imports from any other country, without any previous consultation, for the remainder of 1948, and even then, if we are hard pressed for the currency of a particular country, it is possible by consultation to correct our exchange position by shutting off imports from the country whose cash we require.

If we have made any international commitments, secret or open, to close the Canadian market equally to all nations, regardless of whether they buy from us or not, and regardless of what they buy from us, then in common sense let us relieve ourselves of that obligation to treat all countries alike whether they are customers of ours or not, and let us do it at once.
Schedule I of the bill covers a wide variety of consumer goods, many of which are produced and available in Canada, and their entry to Canada is prohibited from all countries, not from the United States alone. As the Minister of Finance has expressed himself on all occasions as opposed to the continuance of price controls the Canadian consumer is therefore left to the rubber consciences of Canadian industrialists and distributors of the items in schedule I, such as fresh grapes, pears, peas, tomatoes, cocoa, paint, varnish, stoves, sewing machines, typewriters, furniture and so on. At one time I believe that even yeast was on this list, but it has been removed, as have certain types of oils. Evidently the list was carelessly and hurriedly assembled within the Department of Finance. Every item that I have mentioned in schedule I could be imported from Great Britain and countries other than the United States, were it not for the nondiscriminatory policy enunciated by the Minister of Finance on behalf of his government a month ago. And so the minister has left the Canadian public to the sense of price justice, shall we say, of the Canadian distributors of all the articles in schedule I of Bill No. 3.
Why did not the minister impose the most rigorous price controls, and even rationing if necessary, on the articles in schedule I? Before dealing with some of the specific measures contained in the bill, I wish to make a few general remarks about conditions that have helped to bring about the present dollar crisis. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), speaking in this house before the Christmas recess, likened the present crisis to that which developed in this country in 1940 when we had a flight of capital from Canada to the United States, and he reminded the house how at that time the Hyde Park agreement was formulated under which we pooled our resources with the United States and large quantities of Canadian exports were paid for with United States dollars for re-export to Europe. In that way we built up our reserves of United States currency.
Ever since the end of the war we in this group have urged from time to time the reimplementing in a modified form of the Hyde Park agreement in order that we might be in a position to balance our payments with the United States, while at the same time providing Europe with the goods that they require. I think it is a sad commentary on world affairs that nations mobilize and pool their resources for common use against an enemy, in order to achieve a common objective, but as soon as the war ends, these nations are no longer prepared to pool their resources in order to establish conditions that are conducive to peace. Nations unite for wholesale destruction; therefore it is absolutely essential that they shall unite in order to repair the damage done during war.
For example, when the capital of a nation which it has taken generations to build up is destroyed almost overnight, does anyone seriously think that nation can or even should be responsible for repairing the damage? I would say it is the joint responsibility of all the countries that participated in the destruction. To suggest that the nation in which the destruction has taken place should repair the damage is to suggest that the standard of living of that country be reduced to so low a level that it may well face anarchy. That is exactly what is happening to many parts of Europe today.
The great tragedy of the post-war years was, I think, the failure of the United States of America to give real leadership. Instead, they cancelled all forms of mutual aid and lend-lease on the day of victory, and from then on made loans conditional upon the signing of certain international agreements heavily

I think we can also say we are seeing the consequences of the agreements in France today.
Apparently at last the planners, or financial experts, or whatever you like to call them, of the United States are beginning to realize the futility of trying to make the nations of the world subservient to certain international organizations, so that now it would seem the aim is to be to build up two worlds, and the nations willing to play according to the rules laid down by the United States will receive help under the Marshall plan. The main purpose of this bill is to conserve foreign exchange, chiefly, as far as we are concerned, to conserve United States dollars, and second, to make Canada more self-sufficient. We in this group agree 100 per cent with both these aims, but we do not by any means agree with a number of the provisions contained in the bill. We do not agree that this is the logical way to reach these objectives.
As I understand the present situation in the world, it is this. Current transactions are approximately in balance. That was true for 1947; but we suffered a serious deficiency in our current transactions with the United States, while at the same time having a large favourable balance with the other nations of the world. I believe that, internally, supply is somewhat lagging behind demand in several lines, but we are now informed by the retail trade that already inventories are being built up in many lines. People are having to draw heavily upon their savings, and instalment buying is steadily increasing today, showing that there is not a surplus of purchasing power in the hands of many people in Canada at the

present time, so that there is not the same inflationary pressure on prices today that there was three years ago.
The logical solution to the international situation'-and' I think the minister would agree to this-would appear to be to expand our exports to the United States or to reduce our imports from that country. That is why we find quite a vigorous demand in western Canada for removal of the embargo on the export of agricultural products to the United States. The farmers feel that, since there is a shortage of United States dollars in Canada, the logical thing would be to allow them to export goods to the United States; and of course there is also the other incentive, that prices of agricultural products in the United States are higher than in Canada, and the farmers would like the benefits of that higher market. I understand that the main reason the government do not approve this suggestion is that they consider we would not be in a position to fulfil our commitments to Europe and at the same time have goods available for export to the United States. I would agree that since the need in Europe is so much greater than in the United States, it is only right that we should fulfil our commitments to Europe.
That being the case, it is absolutely essential that we do everything in our power to increase our imports from Britain. They have many lines of goods available for export, goods which are in demand in this country. Shortly before Christmas I noticed a list published in the Journal showing a long line of goods Britain had available for export, goods we need in this country but which were on the prohibited list. That is why I cannot understand the government placing a prohibition against the importation of certain goods from England, when those goods are available for export. I am aware of the excuse given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), that, since we have placed prohibitions against imports from the United States, therefore we must impose similar prohibitions against imports from other countries, because it is necessary to live up to the principles embodied in the Geneva trade pact. Yet I say I cannot understand the attitude of the government, because we do not have to take such action under the Geneva trade pact. That pact contains an escape clause in article XIV, which states that when a nation has an unfavourable balance of trade with another nation it may place restrictions upon imports from that nation without at the same time having to place similar restrictions upon imports from other countries with which it

There is no doubt that this escape clause was put in for a definite purpose, and' I say that purpose was to deal with exactly the situation we have in 'Canada today. I find it very hard to understand the attitude of some of the officials of the Department of Finance who deal with our international financial agreements. I think we might well investigate to ascertain where the real loyalty of some of these men rests. Does it rest with Wall Street or does it rest with Canada? I am not making that charge in any loose way. We have in the Bretton Woods agreement, the international monetary fund, the Geneva trade pact, certain clauses which are undoubtedly weighted in favour of the United States and detrimental to Canada; yet apparently we feel obliged to agree to them just because the United States is pushing us.

to our taking that action, they may require or ask that we reduce the amount of the subsidy.

It has signed an agreement which definitely limits, in principle, its right or ability to stabilize agricultural prices in the future.
Let me at this point say a few words regarding devaluation of the dollar. As the leader of this group stated in his speech, we think the government made a mistake when it placed the dollar at parity; because, no matter how the minister may argue at the present time, he will admit it has always been understood that when a currency is devalued it has a tendency to encourage exports and to discourage imports. That is the general tendency, although it might not actually apply at the present time. However, if it has any influence, either one way or another, it will be to encourage exports and to discourage imports.	.
I noticed that in his speech the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) says that he supported parity because it reduces the prices of imports. But when he says that, I suggest he is forgetting that trade is a two-way street. When you appreciate a currency you reduce the price of your imports, but you also reduce the price of your exports. Ft is well tQ remember that in Canada over thirty per cent of the people are engaged in agriculture, and that by this policy you may reduce the price of agricultural exports. I cannot see why the farmers of this country should be called upon to subsidize the consumer. There has been altogether too much of that kind of thing, particularly during the war. The farmers have received very little recognition for the sacrifices they made in that connection.
We have only to go back to the thirties to realize how retaining the value of the dollar at a high level penalizes the farmers of this country. In the thirties the Canadian dollar was appreciated about twenty per cent above the pound sterling, while at the same time the currencies of our competitors were depreciated about twenty-five per cent below sterling, with the result that in a time of keen competition Australia, New Zealand and the Argentine had a forty-five cent advantage over us in price. Minister of Trade and Commerce, say in this house last December, at page 386 of Hansard:
If you look back at the debates in parliament in those days-
He was referring to the war days.
-you will find no carping opposition to the efforts of the government to meet a situation which was similar to the one we are contending with now.
Obviously he did not want any opposition to this program. But there are very good reasons why it is not getting unanimous support either here in the house or in the country, and I propose to outline six of the reasons. No doubt there are many others, but to me these six are the most important.
The first is this. The policy applies against imports from all countries, as I have said, both the dollar countries and the sterling countries. It applies to all countries in the world. That is what the government calls a policy of non-discrimination, yet it is perfectly clear that the problem to be met is the shortage of United States dollars, and it is just as clear that that calls for measures against the United States dollar. Whether we like it or not, measures against the United States dollar are required to meet this emergency, and that means discrimination. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the policy to meet this emergency must of necessity be a policy of discrimination. Yet the government adopts a policy of non-discrimination. We find that quite freely admitted, there is no attempt to conceal it in the short title which I read; and in the description in the bill itself, the government refers to foreign exchange resources, there is no reference to United States dollars, the bill is to cover all exchange. Further, the total prohibition applies to goods of all countries, and the Minister of Finance, in making his speech on the bill, actually went so far as to say that because he had to have a non-discriminatory policy some goods were not prohibited which might otherwise have been, the reason being that the government did not want to be too hard on the sterling countries. That will be found at page 332 of Hansard, where the minister said:
Since the principle of non-discrimination involved application of the prohibitions to all countries, the list naturally does not include items which are of considerable importance to countries to which we have been extending credits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In other words we selected the prohibited items as carefully as possible.

You could have prohibited further goods from the United States if you had been dealing only with United States goods.

Then there is the quota applicable to all countries, although there is a sly loophole in connection with that quota. Under the order in council now in effect there are what are called scheduled and non-scheduled countries, and different treatment is given to these two groups, also the quota is based on the years before the war, the purpose apparently being to ease the situation with regard to imports from Great Britain.
Finally, capital goods, as I have said, can come in only under permit from all countries. Why, I ask the minstry, is that provision directed against the members of the British commonwealth and against the nations to which we have lent money, all of which are anxious to send us their goods? The answer to that question contains my second objection to this program. It is this. Obviously this non-discriminatory policy was either dictated from Washington or designed to curry favour at Washington. The Minister of Finance said, at page 332 of Hansard:
Knowing their views and subscribing to the same principle ourselves, it was only reasonable that we should make a special effort to avoid direct discriminatory practices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a pretty fair statement.

He said the same thing with regard to the prohibition of goods from countries not in the dollar area. Those remarks will be found at page 95 of Hansard:
The Minister of Reconstruction, now also the Minister of Trade and Commerce, said that Canadian production was now to be tailored to fit United States production, his words will be found at page 389 of Hansard; and the excise taxes were placed on goods manufactured solely from Canadian products, the reason being given that that helps the United States to hold her market for these goods in Canada.
Mr. -ABBOTT: That was not the only reason.

That statement was made by the Minister of Finance and will be found at page 336 of Hansard, where he said:
But by imposing these excise taxes we are doing something to protect the legitimate longer-range interests of these businesses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend wanted me to correct him where he was wrong. If he will go on and read the other part of my remarks he will see that there was an additional reason, that the primary reason was to reduce the consumption of Canadian goods having a significant United States dollar import content.

One of the reasons was to stop the consumption of goods produced in Canada containing parts brought in from the United. States, but the other reason he gave was the one I have mentioned, to hold the market for United States goods; and I am complaining, Mr. Speaker, because that provision was made in respect of goods manufactured in Canada which contain solely Canadian materials.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said this was not put in as a protectionist measure, and it is not.

It is a lot worse than that. It is a measure to protect the interests of the United States, not the interests of Canada. This policy shows an amazing subservience to the United States. One would think Canada was a subject country. No Canadian government since confederation has ever gone so far toward taking orders from the government of another country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is rubbish. We take no orders from anyone.

The policy is worse than
rubbish. It is a terribly tragic policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When my hon. friend says that we are taking orders from another country, he is talking rubbish.
The minister can. make his speech in his own good time. I am making my speech now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But my hon. friend1 asked me to correct him when he made an inaccurate statement of facts.

Contrast the attitude taken by this government with the attitude taken by Mr. Bennett when, as prime minister of this country, he negotiated the empire trade treaties here in Ottawa. There was none of this kowtowing and cringing to another country. Canada took her place at the conference table with the other nations of the commonwealth beside her and debated trade questions man-to-man fashion. There was none of this business of Canada fawning on the United States. There was none of that sort of thing in 1932.
Canadians are a very proud people, and rightly so. I would remind the Minister of Finance and other hon. members of the part that Canadians played in the two great world wars. There was not a Canadian in uniform in either of those wars who did not consider he was just as good as or a little better than the man from any other country. I repeat: we are a very proud people. Now we are being

Foreign Exchange Conservation
humiliated by our own government. Canada will never become a great world power on policies of this kind. That is my second reason for saying that this program does not have the support of the Canadian people.
A third reason for the non-support is that the policy endangers our trade with the nondollar countries of the world. This trade is very important even at the present time when they are struggling to get back on their feet.
I hold in my hand a publication entitled " Foreign Trade," put out by the Department of Trade and Commerce; the issue of December 6, 1947. From it I find that during the first nine months of 1947 Canadian exports to the United States were valued at $732,979,000; while our exports to empire countries were higher, being valued at $845,518,000. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, now Minister of Trade and Commerce, and presumably soon to be Minister of Mines and Resources as well, made a statement on January 22 in which he is quoted to the effect that for the whole of 1947, 37 per cent of our exports went to the United States, 27 per cent to the United Kingdom and 15 per cent to other empire and commonwealth countries, showing that for the full year exports to the British countries exceeded exports to the United States. It is only natural that that should be so because Canada and the United States produce largely the same products, and there will always be competition between us. For example, on the Pacific coast our lumber has to compete with lumber from Washington and Oregon. Our apples have to compete with apples from these two American states. On the prairies our grain products have to compete with the grain products of the United States prairie states; Ontario and Quebec manufactured products must compete with those of the industrial eastern states, and in the maritime provinces our fishery products compete with the same type of products from the New England states; whereas in Great Britain, in Australia, and in other members of the commonwealth and France the products for sale are not the same type of products that we produce ourselves, and there is naturally greater scope for trade. Yet actually, in spite of the importance of this non-dollar trade, the Minister of Finance wants exports diverted to the United States. I quote from page 329 of Hansard, the speech that the minister made on December 16, in which he said:
Considerable further expansion in our United States dollar exports can be achieved by diverting exports away from other countries and by reducing Canadian consumption.
In other words, he appears to be deliberately breaking down trade with these non-dollar nations. I submit it is obvious to every hon.

member that if there is to be any diversion in our export trade it should be the other way, away from the dollar countries to the nondollar countries, thereby cutting down our reliance on United States goods. Yet no stress whatever has been placed by any minister of this government on buying elsewhere than in the United States. One would have thought this was a great-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did, in my speech.
The minister did not say much about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Look up the speech.

One would have thought the situation would give us a grand chance to get goods elsewhere. Instead of that, we find Canada now trying to break into the United States market with manufactured goods; and, believe me, that is a tough proposition, as every hon. member should know.
The minister of half the portfolios made a statement to that effect yesterday in Toronto, I believe, in which he emphasized the need for Canada getting our manufactured products into the United States market. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), who has been out on a leadership campaign emphasized the same thing in Winnipeg. This is the heading we find:
U.S. Need Held Exports Goal
St. Laurent urges increased production of required goods.
Winnipeg, Jan. 23. Increased production of commodities which have a market in the United States was urged here tonight by Rt. Hon. Louis St. Laurent as a measure to increase Canada's dollar receipts.
I am doubtful whether a policy of that type can be made successful. We have heard that the government is relying on the Marshall plan. The Marshall plan is not going to help Canada to get her products into the United States. The very best that the Marshall plan can do is to buy Canadian products with United States money to send to Europe. That will not be of any help in getting our products into the United States market.
The Minister of Finance said something about getting a further treaty with the United States. He is going to ask the Americans to cut their tariff beyond the provisions of the Geneva treaty so that we can get more of our products into the United States. I hold in my hand a press dispatch of January 11 which appeared in the Herald Tribune, and which reads as follows:
U.S. is claimed cool to tariff cut tries.
New York, Jan. 11. The Herald Tribune said today in a financial page story that the United States state department had showed only

Foreign Exchange Conservation
"polite" interest in efforts by the Canadian government to initiate new trade agreements with the United States.	.
The newspaper said that it was learned in New York that there appears little likelihood that Canadian proposals to open conversations looking to further reductions of trade barriers will advance beyond the study stage by state department officials.
On the same day the Minister of Finance was asked what he thought about the press dispatch, and the heading for his reply was: "Ottawa is hopeful."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I said.

The article reads:
Ottawa is "Hopeful"
Ottawa, Jan. 11. Finance Minister Abbott said tonight the Canadian government was "hopeful" for new trade agreements with the United States, and already had made known its attitude to Washington.
Well, I think before Canada gets very much further along the road we should be going we shall have to have a government that is a good deal more than hopeful about some of these questions.
Another reason the policy is not one that has the support of the Canadian people is the uncertainty, uncertainty in so many aspects. First of all, there is uncertainty as to how long this policy is to be in effect. The government brings in a drastic policy affecting the lives of thousands of Canadian people, and one minister, the minister of half the portfolios, said:
My experience tells me that if we will make the building up of United States dollar exports a national objective, we should be able to balance our trade in a matter of months, and on a high level, rather than on a restricted level.
This quotation is taken from the minister's radio adress of November 20 of last year. More recently the Minister of Finance comes along and on January 9 we get this from him. From New York the minister is reported as having said as follows:
Abbott sees no end near for dominion's austerity.
Canada's Finance Minister Douglas Abbott sees no end to "austerity" in the near future. He said today it depends on results achieved this winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. I did not use the phrase "no end".

If there had been a set period of time Canadian businessmen would have known exactly what to face.
Then take the treatment handed' out to the automobile dealers, just as an illustration. The Minister of Finance said in his radio address on November 17 with regard to the total prohibition of automobiles:
We are also, at the outset, prohibiting temporarily the importation of all motor vehicles,
but we intend in the near future to replace this complete prohibition with a restrictive quota system.
In the meantime these dealers have been cut off from the United States production and from the British. Two months have gone by-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They got a lot in before the change was made.

Two months have gone by and the government is still fooling around and has not decided on the quota. This means in effect that these dealers are being run out of business, in addition to which, of course, they have had a terrific excise tax imposed on their product.
Then take the terms of the bill itself. Provision is made in the bill for drastic changes.
I will not go into the sections, but we find extremely wide powers to switch products from one schedule to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Always relaxing them.

The excise taxes have been changed half a dozen times already since the policy was announced.
Another reason for uncertainty is the demand made on Canadian manufacturers to produce goods for the United States market. The ministers say to the Canadian producer, "Go out and produce goods for the United States market". Take the man who has been producing articles for the Canadian or the British market. He does not know what to produce for the United States market, and the ministers do not know either. They are just hoping. It all adds up to uncertainty, and that uncertainty arises largely from the fact that the ministry brought in a program without knowing what they intended to do. Their program was half-baked. It was never properly thought out before it was announced.
Not even half-baked.
Perhaps quarter-baked.
Not baked at all.

The fifth reason why the policy has not won support is that the small man is kicked around unmercifully. I know that in my own city of Vancouver many a businessman cannot make a living because of this program. These men are receiving letters from the officials of the department concerned telling them to be good Canadians; that is what they are getting out on the coast. The small businessman cannot afford to come to Ottawa. He cannot take the time or pay the money to come here, and if he did come he could not get the situation remedied anyway.
