There should be officials in British Columbia able to make on-the-spot decisions in these cases, and the same provision should be made for the maritime provinces and the prairies.
Then take the quotas. First of all, there was a delay in establishing many of the quotas, which made things frightfully difficult for the businessmen concerned1; further, the quotas were set on the basis of business done for the year preceding June 30, 1947, which meant that people who had only started up in business during that period were out of luck. A large number of these men were veterans, young men coming back from the fighting forces, and they were just getting started in business. These men find that because quotas are based on that period they are not able to get sufficient goods to carry on. That is very unfair.
Another way in which the small man is kicked around is in punitive taxation, these heavy excise taxes. I do not need to give examples, but I would mention electrical appliances. It always seems to me that this Minister of Finance lives in the horse-and-buggy days; whenever his budget comes down, whenever there is anyone to be soaked, the first one to get it is the man dealing in electrical appliances, or the young veteran and his wife who want to buy such appliances in order to set up housekeeping. Alw'ays you find electrical appliances being included in any of these heavy taxation measures.
The final example of the kicking around of the small man was what happened at the United States border when this policy was put into effect. South of Vancouver, people who had left Canada a day or two before, without knowing at all that this plan was to come in, made purchases not exceeding $100, as they were perfectly at liberty to do; when they got back to the boundary on November 18 they were told by officials of the government, "You have to go back with these goods. Take them back to the store or give them away or throw them away. You cannot bring them across the border." That is the way the thing was handled at that point, and it even went to the length of sealing the dining car on the Great Northern railway running from Seattle to Vancouver. That is inexcusable in any country not run by a dictatorship.
I say that the rights of the small Canadian have been trampled underfoot in this program.
My final reason for non-support of the program is the dictatorial powers given the minister-and I am looking right at the minister who has half of the portfolios. We find him given wide powers. It does not say what minister is to administer the bill. They

can be switched. One minister can handle one commodity and the other something else, just as the government sees fit. This minister to whom I refer I have seen, in my period in the house, dictator of national harbours, then dictator of radio, dictator of aviation, of atomic energy and of the maritime commission; heading the Department of Reconstruction, with over-riding powers over all other departments of government, and now trade and commerce, which means the wheat business in Canada and our external trade. Further, we find a press dispatch of January 24 carrying the headline:
Broadening of Howe powers on mines, resources, trade, reported next Ottawa move.
This is quite apart from the personality of the minister concerned. He may be the best minister in the whole world-
Hear, hear.

It seems to me that the
government thinks he is the only minister in Canada who is any good at all. This trend is very dangerous and is caused by the failure of the cabinet to deal with problems as they arise; the situation will go from bad to worse; the only way to remedy it is to defeat the government, and that is what the Canadian people will do at the next election. The smiles across the way look pretty sickly.
In the meantime, the Canadian people have this Abbott austerity program firmly fastened on their necks in a last minute endeavour by the government to get out of a bad situation into which the nation was allowed to drift; by a government which paid no heed to the warnings that were given and ignored every danger signal.
The ministers have been trying to get by through following a policy of doing nothing, as they have done on so many occassions before. One other good example was the way they tried to get by on the reinforcement question in 1944; this same tribe that we have sitting opposite us today. They have failed utterly to give leadership, and without leadership, Mr. Speaker, Canada or any other nation is bound to founder.

Mr. Speaker, on November 17 of last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made an important statement over the radio, following a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. JANUARY 26, 1948
______________Foreign Exchange Conservation
Mackenzie King) setting the provisions, the hopes and the aspirations of the Geneva trade agreement. Those who listened to the two broadcasts that evening were momentarily confused because of their contradictory nature, and now it appears that for a great many this confusion has become complete chaos. Since that date we have been waiting to see in statutory form what the government had in mind in the way of restrictions on imports in their effort to conserve their reserves of United States currency. It is now January 26, and we have before us Bill No. 3. Anyone who attempts to make head or tail of this bill, especially since every day when you pick up your newspaper you find that some detail of government policy is being changed, gets the impression that he is trying to follow a bewildering charade of some sort. There does not seem to be any sense of reality to it. At a time when this country and the world have been made conscious of the need for free trade, or at least freer trade than we have had so far, suddenly we are faced with restrictions and prohibitions on imports from the United States, so all-embracing that the government has found it necessary to change its policy several times since the announcement was made.
The point with which I am most concerned tonight is the effect this bill will have on the people of western Canada, if it becomes legislation, though I am not unmindful of the effect it will have on the whole population of Canada. For example, if you examine the position of the farmers of the west you will find that this is just one more of the many crippling pieces of legislation, put into effect by this government, which have hit the farmers. I should like to quote briefly from the Winnipeg Free Press of January 6, 1948. I could quote from other newspapers, but I have chosen the Free Press because it is not notoriously anti-government, and perhaps its opinion will be taken as authentic. In discussing the effect of these prohibitions and restrictions on western agriculture, that newspaper had this to say in an editorial:
The prairie farmer is shut out of the prosperous United States market. His income is limited by law. But there is no limit on the prices he must pay for any goods he buys and the events now under way assure that these prices will go up.
The events referred to are the restrictions and prohibitions. Then the editorial goes on:
Prices generally are moving up, of course, all over North America but there is now a new and special reason for their rise in Canada. With United States supplies of many articles cut off or reduced by import restrictions, a new, lush, preserve of protection has been carved out for Canadian industry.
Then, to top it off, the editorial goes on:
In the past the west was penalized indirectly by high tariffs and discriminatory freight rates. Now a penalty is added in the form of a limit of income, while, at the same time prices are going up, aided in their ascent by a new protection.
I noticed today that the Minister of Finance objected when one of the speakers described this legislation as a new form of protection, and said it was not meant to be protection. Perhaps it was not, but we can judge only by the effect it will have, whatever the intentions; and to my mind it is the most rabid type of protectionism we have ever had in this country. Even the most Tory of the governments we have had in the past never produced legislation which was half as protectionist as this will be if it ever comes into effect. What does it do? It shuts out imports of manufactured articles from the United States, covering practically the whole gamut of commodities used by the people of Canada. At the same time there is a shortage in Canada, so that Canadian industries are given not only a free hand to sell their products but also an artificial shortage on top of the actual Shortage that exists, and in this way they are given an undue advantage over the consumer.
In that regard we find that the farmers of western Canada, who have to sell their wheat under the British agreement and who are denied the export markets of the United States for their cattle and other livestock products, are placed in the position that their markets are restricted, their income is restricted, but the things they have to buy are protected so that they will have to pay any price Canadian industry wants to charge. I believe restrictions and prohibitions such as these, when not accompanied by a system of price control, are most unfair and discriminatory, particularly against western agriculture.
We find also that, while the government have been talking of doing something about the high cost of living and about bringing down prices, under this program designed to conserve United States dollars they have placed an excise tax of up to twenty-five per cent on certain articles. The result is, of course, that if a person must buy those articles he must pay that extra fifteen or twenty-five per cent, as the case may be, and the cost of living is shoved up that much higher. It would be understandable if the government were to tell the people of Canada that more money must be raised by means of an excise tax in order to pay for greater social services,

Foreign Exchange Conservation
or some other government expenditure which would be for the benefit of all the people. Then those buying such goods would know the tax would be devoted to a useful purpose. But the Minister of Finance told the people of Canada on November 17 that the excise tax was not being imposed for the purpose of raising money but for the purpose of discouraging purchases. I want to say to the minister in all sincerity that those in the low-income groups-and he knows they comprise a very large majority of the people of Canada -are already prohibited from buying goods which are priced too high for their budget. The addition of an extra twenty-five per cent to that price will only have the effect of making it still harder for those people to get the necessities of life, while those who have plenty of money will not be discouraged in the least because they will have the wherewithal to buy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the tax is not imposed on necessities.

The minister says the tax is not imposed on necessities. Well, we could get into quite a discussion as to what is and what is not a necessity, but let me point to one example. Let us take automobiles. The minister may not think an automobile is a necessity. He may have the advantage of living in a city, where he can jump on a streetcar and reach his destination in a few minutes. But there are a great many people in western Canada, where we have wide open spaces, and where we have to cover long distances; and there are thousands of people in this country who make their living by driving cars. So that it is pretty hard to say which things are necessities and which are not. The minister may say that liquor is a necessity; I notice it is not on the prohibited list. So it is clear that we have a difference of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: People are still spending a lot of money on liquor.

I have no doubt that all hon. members, day after day, are receiving letters from various business concerns, including retailers and other groups, about goods which they consider are certainly not luxuries, but are necessities.
For instance, let us consider sporting goods. Canada is one of the most sport-conscious nations of the world, and we consider certain types of sporting goods, such as skis, skates, baseball bats, footballs and other sporting equipment, not as luxuries, but as one of the most important types of commodities for the improvement of the health and opportunity of the young people of Canada. I would not

classify them as a luxury; they are a necessity. Yet we have an excise tax which discourages the young people of Canada from taking the full advantage of sporting life which should be available to them.
Then, I would refer to fresh fruits and vegetables, another class of commodities upon which restrictions have been placed. I do not believe even the minister will argue that fruits and vegetables are a luxury. People know that without them our diet cannot be kept in proper balance, and that in the end it may cost us more money through doctor bills if we try to economize in the use of these essential foods.
I hold in my hand letters similar to those which I have no doubt have been received by other hon. members, containing petitions from retail merchants and other people across Canada, in which they seek the .removal of these restrictions on the importation of fruits and vegetables. For example, I have before me a letter which was written by the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, with head office in Winnipeg. The letter points out that for some reason or an other Winnipeg has been picked as a victim of these restrictions on fruits and vegetables. They say they have been discriminated against, perhaps more than any other city in Canada.
With this in mind they have addressed a letter to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I refer to it only because the hon. member has already exhausted his right to speak in the debate. Otherwise undoubtedly he would have brought it up himself. They have this to say:
*Residents in the province of Manitoba have been particularly hard hit by the embargo on produce and our association has been receiving complaints from all sources-jobbers, wholesalers, retailers and consumers. Even our local growers approve imports, realizing that our growing season and storage facilities are inadequate to supply green vegetables in sufficient quantities to meet the demand throughout the winter months.
The city of Winnipeg health department has endorsed the general protest and, in order to provide the consumers' viewpoint, we attach letters which have been signed by customers of local stores. These letters are being received daily from Winnipeg and rural districts and are representative of the opinion of Manitoba residents as a whole.
They attach a list of about 400 names in which they petition as follows, as set out in a telegram on January 19, 1948, addressed to the Minister of Finance:
At a meeting with Canada-wide representation of national foods officers of the retail merchants' association of Canada held here today the following resolution was adopted for submission to you: "Whereas the domestic supply of cabbage, lettuce, spinach and celery is ex-

Foreign Exchange Conservation
hausted in most parts of Canada and whereas these essential health foods are available for importation at reasonable prices be it resolved that the government be urged to provide for their immediate importation in order to protect the health of the nation as well as reducing the cost of living thereby."
This is signed by the retail merchants' association of Canada. This is only one example of the pleas being sent to the government to use some common sense in the restrictions and prohibitions imposed upon the people of Canada.
I should like now to refer to another phase of this legislation to which reference has already been made by two hon. members, and particularly by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who made a most excellent case on this particular point. I refer to the application of the so-called non-discrimination clause as agreed to in the Geneva pact. I should like at this time to quote something to which reference was made by the hon. member for Acadia, and that is article XIV, section 6 (a) of the general agreement. It states:
That the provisions of the agreement relating to non-discrimination shall not come into force in respect of import restrictions applied by any contracting party ... in order to safeguard its external financial position and balance of payments, until January 1, 1949; provided that this period may, with the concurrence of the contracting parties, be extended for such further periods as they may specify in respect of any contracting party whose supply of convertible currency is inadequate . . .
What do we find? We find that apparently because the United States wishes to have the non-discrimination clause strictly observed, in spite of the fact that the agreement itself does not impose that obligation upon the Canadian government, that government has, as well as restricting goods from the United States to conserve our dollar position, placed the same restrictions on other imports from other countries. It places us in a ridiculous position because we have shipped to other countries much more than we have been able to get back in return, by way of goods. We have shipped these goods to European countries, including Great Britain. This means that they owe us a great deal of money which they can pay only by shipping goods to us.
At the same time we owe goods to the United States. So what do we do? Instead of accepting goods from European countries and exporting more to the United States, thus balancing our false position, we restrict importation from all countries and, by some magic, expect that that will solve our dollar problem.
I have a list here which shows what we could have imported from countries other than the United States. However, we have failed to take advantage of article XIV, section 6(a)
of the general agreement, which permits us to do so. For example, I would mention fresh grapes from the Argentine and Chile; fresh pears from Australia, the Argentine and Chile; green peas from Mexico, and fresh tomatoes from the Bahamas and Mexico.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All for United States dollars though.

Cocoa and chocolate
powder from the United Kingdom; paints and varnishes from the United Kingdom, Norway and France.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are under quota.
Stoves, sewing machines, typewriters .and furniture from the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You cannot get them.
Onions from Chile and Egypt; textiles, leather, cutlery, clocks and watches from the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every yard of textiles that they will send us can be brought in. There is no restriction upon the importation of textiles.

If the minister is going to argue both sides of the case, he is welcome to do so; and perhaps he can do so. But on the one hand he is trying to tell us that these goods are restricted so that they cannot come in, while on the other he is telling us that they are coming in to the full extent possible. Well, if they are coming in to the full extent why place a restriction on them? If there is no desire to restrict importations from these countries, why include them in this bill? Apparently there is no answer to that.
If we examine the bill carefully and all the events leading up to it we must come to the conclusion that it is an attempt-and not the first one-by the government, to tie us up completely with the economy of the United States. It is putting the economy of Canada into a strait-jacket and, as was so well said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), it places Canada in a subservient position vis-a-vis the United States. I see no reason for that.
Of course the minister and his supporters, his apologists, will say that we cannot afford to offend the United States, that we must kowtow to the United States because we cannot obtain oil and other necessities elsewhere. We should not always be carrying our hat in our hands when we go bargaining. We should not forget that the United States obtains some of her essentials in Canada, one example being paper. If the United States were not able to obtain pulp and paper from

Foreign Exchange Conservation
Canada more than half of their journals and newspapers would have to cease publication. An hon. member here mentions nickel, and asbestos is another example. There are many basic products which the United States must obtain in Canada. I am not saying that we want to make a bad neighbour of ourself because that is not necessary. We should have some self-respect. We should not bow our necks to the United States even before they ask us to do so.
There is another feature of this proposed legislation which is quite objectionable. It places in the hands of several ministers complete power to make decisions and to discriminate according to their judgment, good or bad as it may be, with regard to quotas and restrictions. I believe that is one of the most objectionable things about the bill. Not only are the ministers given a blank cheque to do as they like, but the jurisdiction of this bill is scattered among several departments. The average person will have to be a sort of Philadelphia lawyer to figure out which department he should go to.
I have an advertisement in my hand-I do not know the date of it but it is quite recent- signed by the Minister of Finance and headed, "Answering your questions about import control." I believe this appeared in most of the newspapers. It goes on to tell the people of Canada where they should go to-that is a rather good phrase-in order to find out where to get a permit, how much the quota will be and so on. It says that if you are an importer and wish to import goods subject to quota, if you wish information about your quota, you are to go to such-and-such a department. There are a lot of "ifs" about it, which is characteristic of the legislation of this government.
The first one tells you to go to the Department of National Revenue. The next one tells you to go to the Department of Finance. Then reference is made to the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. I suppose, since the reshuffle, it will be the Department of Trade and Commerce, which is not mentioned here. A new advertisement will have to be published pretty soon; this one is out of date already. Then further on, if you please, we find it involves the Department of National Health and Welfare. Can you imagine that department having anything to do with trade and commerce? However, there it is.
Of course the minister will say that this is unavoidable because these things involve these different departments and you cannot place them all under the one minister. I agree with him to that extent because they do concern these different departments. It appears to me

that there is only one sensible course to take under these circumstances and that is to set up an import-export board to co-ordinate all these departments which are affected by this legislation. It is hopeless to expect the people of Canada to understand all the intricacies, all the maze and webwork of red tape involved in visits to these various departments and the getting in touch with different officials. This country is too large and complex to be governed entirely from Ottawa.
The government should set up an export-import board which would be non-partisan in nature and be able to give everybody fair treatment. It could co-ordinate the ramifications of this measure as they affect various departments of government. Then the people of this country would have one central agency to which they could go to make application or to get information and so on.
One can imagine the complete state of confusion we would have had during the war if the wartime prices and trade board had been scattered among six, seven or ten different departments. Any person having any problem to bring up would have had to run around from one official to another. But we had just the one board which made decisions and consulted the various departments as they were affected. Surely if that were a sensible way of doing that job it would be a sensible way of doing this one.
More than that, if it were done in that way it would be possible for the government to plan a certain amount of our future trade. Regardless of what political point of view we may have, I think it is inescapable that a certain amount of planning must be done in the future so far as trade is concerned. I do not care whether one possesses the point of view of a free enterpriser, or a private enterpriser as they call themselves; I do not care whether one believes in private or public enterprise, it is unavoidable that there will have to be a certain amount of planning and direction in the future in connection with trade. That will be necessary because so many countries in the world are working on that basis. If we are to trade with them we shall have to work on that basis too.
If we had an export-import board it would be able to do some intelligent planning so far as our trade is concerned. As the situation is now, we find that private industry-I am not saying this in any derogatory way-is substituting its own type of planning for the kind of planning that national governments should be doing. In other words, in effect they are saying to the governments of the world, "If you will not plan your trade for the welfare of the general public, then, we shall plan our trade

for our own benefit and you will have to take the consequences." I am not saying that just because I want to; the evidence is there. If you turn to the McGregor report on international cartels you will find this on page 20:
Canadian Industries Limited is restricted by its parent companies. I.C.I. and Dupont to operation in Canada and "is not to engage in any export trade even when it is in a favourable position to do so through tariff preference and other causes."
Note it is the I.C.I. and Dupont who are giving the orders to Canadian Industries Limited, it is not the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Finance. No department of government apparently has as much power and direction over the trade of Canadian Industries Limited as have Dupont and I.C.I. How are we to plan intelligently in connection with trade in this country when someone in another country has control over a subsidiary in this country? Another example is to be found on page 25 of the same report where he deals with the production and manufacture and distribution of matches. He says:
The policy was decided by the cartel members outside Canada that Canadian production should be sold only in Canada while they refrained from exporting matches to Canada.
Note that it says it is decided by the cartel members outside Canada that Canadian production should be confined to Canada. There you have an almost unbelievable situation, private industry outside the borders of this country dictating to industries in this country as to what they may export and where. We are asked to approve a bill which is supposed to be a measure to conserve our foreign exchange position. What is the use of our passing legislation and giving ourselves the illusion of being masters of the situation when, as a matter of fact, industries outside this country which are not subject to our laws are in a position to dictate who shall export and what they shall export. In the conclusion of his report the commissioner says:
However, the volume of our trade may be limited by the cartel so that expansion of Canadian industries may be slower than it would be if exports were made without restriction. The conditions imposed by the cartel agreement may run counter to Canadian trade policy-
That is straight from the shoulder. We may make our own trade policy and pass legislation, but international cartels not subject to our laws can make rules which run counter to our legislation, and they can get away with it. The commissioner goes on:
-but if our exporters are to secure the advantages they see in the agreement they will be forced to follow the policy adopted by members of the cartel rather than Canadian government trade policy.
He concludes by saying:
It is dangerous to have such power of discrimination subject only to the discretion of private interests.
I agree with him wholeheartedly. It is extremely dangerous. As a matter of fact it makes us look ridiculous to pass laws giving the illusion to the Canadian people that we are in charge of the situation when, as a matter of fact, our export and import policies, our whole trade policy, is dictated from beyond the boundaries of this country.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) told us in his speech last December that it was the policy and function of his department to expand Canadian industry and increase production, as his contribution toward solving the United States dollar short-, age. But if he will examine the statement of the commissioner which I have just quoted he will begin to realize that his best laid plans may go completely astray because somebody outside Canada who does not hold two or half a dozen portfolios but does control a few billion dollars may make decisions opposed to his.
I believe that the people of Canada will agree with the Minister of Reconstruction and other members who have spoken of increased Canadian production and greater industrial expansion as the long-range solution of our exchange problem with the United States. There is no easy way out of it. We must produce more in our own country and import less from the United States if we are ever to get out of the debt of that country. That is clear. But I cannot go along with the Minister of Reconstruction and Trade and Commerce, and a few other things, when he tells us that his means of expanding industry and increasing production in this country is by encouraging private industry here to go into certain fields of production. A limited amount may be achieved in that way, but in the long run the government will come to realize, as many people in this country do now, that if we are to have any appreciable expansion of industry in Canada the bulk of it must take place in western Canada.
I am not opposed to industry in eastern Canada, but in the east industry has been expanding for some time and it has not solved our problem. In western Canada we have great possibilities and very little has been done to take advantage of them. There are various reasons for that. Private capital is not disposed to take risks on the expansion of industry in western Canada. While some of our provincial governments in the west, notably those of Saskatchewan and Alberta, have been doing a little on their own hook to get new
Foreign Exchange Conservation

industries started, they have found themselves restricted by jurisdictional powers and by lack of financial resources. I think it is clear that if we are to have any large-scale development of industry in western Canada the initiative will have to be taken by the federal government. I do not know of any better investment that the federal government could now make than to invest in western Canada a few million or a few hundred million dollars, if necessary, to get new industries going to produce so many of the products that we now have to import from the United States. Some small experiments have been made. One is the factory in Portage la Prairie which is processing flax fibre, and other examples could be given. But when you look at the whole picture across the three prairie provinces you will see that the surface has not yet been scratched in comparison with the possibilities of industrial development in those three provinces. That is the long-range solution, and the government of this country should make full use of public investment in those fields where private enterprise has not yet taken advantage of the possibilities.
I realize, of course, that this is contrary to the views and policy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) who, as it happens, just one year ago in addressing the Toronto board of trade said in effect that, so far as he was concerned, the government would) enter into the picture only to fill the gaps in employment and would dio nothing more by way of public investment. I hope that the rest of the cabinet do not share that same narrow point of view.

Mr. Speaker, I did not know that I would be taking part in this debate so soon after the house met; consequently I am not too well prepared. As a matter of fact it is so sudden that I am very anxious to hear what I am going to say. I know the former minister of veterans affairs would not get that. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last November brought forward agreements worked out by toiling experts after several months work we felt that in this plan called the .Geneva trade agreements there were signs of better days ahead through more trade. The first reaction of Canadians, as I found it, was not to find fault with these Geneva agreements but more or less to wait and see, to try it. One sort of formed this opinion as the voice came through on the radio from London, England, and we had a half hour of encouragement, sort of happiness and bliss after the Prime Minister spoke, and those who forgot to shut the radio off heard the voice of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) coming through. You know at home you can shut him off; maybe you cannot do so here. But I did not do it. We listened to him. Some of the newspapers headlined this thing as "Abbott's austerity program." Later in the house the minister said he did not like the word "austerity". Probably he thought it was

smart to borrow it 'because he thought it was becoming fashionable. Later he was sorry he used it.
However, in addition to prohibiting the importation of certain articles, which was a sensible course to pursue to save United States dollars-it takes Canadian dollars to buy them; I found that out-he imposed a twenty-five per cent- excise tax on a multitude of articles recommended by, we will say, theoretical economists or economists, to stop sales of these articles; hence to cut production and perhaps thereby cause unemployment which, of course, would absorb purchasing power, although it is a bad way to do so.
This afternoon I thought this debate was a pretty important thing. I thought all the Liberals would be here waiting to hear and to see. At one time we had fifteen on the opposite benches. At the low it got down to eight. At the real low the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and what have you. was absent.

That is pretty good for me. There are only thirteen from western Ontario; therefore we must have two from Toronto.
In any event, it looked to me as though the Liberal members were ready to acquiesce in anything that the government introduced, willing to acquiesce in any kind of power so long as they stay in power. That is only my own observation.
If the minister did not like this word "austerity" which he said he did not like, in view of all these taxes, this curtailment of production, this curtailment of purchasing power and the increased cost of living, perhaps I can give the program a true label. I was often busy in my day devising labels for merchandise.
How should we label the hon. member?

I will not give the hon.
member his true label but I am labelling the program. I would label i.t for the newspapers, "Abbott's anti-prosperity program" instead of "Abbott's austerity program".
It looks to me as if there were two weddings being attended by the government at the same time. One was the glamorous, beautiful and much publicized royal wedding, and the other was I would say a shot-gun wedding between the United States economists and the Canadian finance officials at which vows were taken that we would put a twenty-five per cent excise tax on the goods we manufactured in Canada which were similar to the goods manufactured in the United States and which we prohibited. Why? To kill the Canadian market for these goods of Canadian manufacturers, to kill the production, if you like, pro tern, until the taxes were removed and these markets would be opened. Naturally this is the result being obtained, as people who have the money to buy these items that are subject to the twenty-five per cent tax are not buying them too profusely, and, of course, the veteran and the working man cannot afford to buy them at these government inflated prices. Officials say, "Oh, well, the tax is neither here nor there. We* hope we do not collect much money from this tax. It will show that the people of Canada are co-operating by not purchasing." At the same time you can see they are co-operating, by reducing their standard of living or by living on relief and unemployment insurance, because their jobs have been destroyed. The way this tax was imposed showed plainly that the imposer was being led up an unknown and untrodden alley by theoretical economists.
I had better stop there and explain my personal interpretation of a theoretical economist. To my way of thinking there are two types of economists. If a man, no matter how small, has opened up a shop on Monday morning, sweeps it out, runs it all week selling goods, handles help and deliveries, pays his bills, pays his payroll on Saturday, takes home the bacon to mama and gives a dollar to church on Sunday, he is a practical economist. He has learned the only practical way. On the other hand, most of those who get jobs as economists handling the biggest business in the world, which is government business, learn it from books in school. I went to school, believe it or not, and the answers were in the back of the book, that so we always knew whether we were right or not before we sent in our problem, if we had an extra book. Those who get jobs as economists look in the back of the book. There is no answer there and they are lost. They dream; they crystal-gaze and they try untried theories. I do not suppose the increasing cost of living and unemployment ever entered their heads. They are too interested in what they are doing. Economists! Surely if this idea had ever entered their heads, the idea of taxing everything would have been thrown into the ashcan. Why, the government already had reported a surplus of $573 million in eight months, and by April 1 they boast they will have the largest surplus any government ever had in Canadian history. I wonder if there is anything symbolic about the date,

April 1? It is April fool's day, you know. It may be taxpayers' day. It may be the day on which they will see the light.
If this upsetting program continues to run, not work-it cannot work-the way it is now, Canada will not only have the largest surplus for years by next April, but have the largest number of unemployed people. This bill, this program, inaugurated without legislation behind the backs of parliament, slipped over on the Canadian public a la hoodwink style after the Prime Minister's royal wedding glow, not only adds to the cost of living but adds to this surplus. So that by April 1 of next year probably SoO for every man, woman and child in Canada will have been taken. In other words, there would have been left in circulation $50 for every man, woman and child in Canada for cost of living purposes.
Now the government has indicated in the last few weeks that it may proceed against profiteers. My hon. friends on the left have recommended it and it is in the statute books. I think they should, but who is the biggest profiteer in Canada when they take S50 from every man, woman and child in the country? When they are making this investigation they had better investigate the government which has put on these taxes. Shame on the government. They should have left them off. They should have removed indirect taxes which pyramid and affect every article figured in the cost of living index. If a manufacturer charges $108 and you include the sales tax, the distributor has to add twenty per cent, or, in other words, it is $129.60 when it leaves him, and so on.
The hidden tax is pyramided and affects the cost of living. It shows that these officials of the government had no idea where they were going or what they were doing, and events since have shown that they did not know what they were doing. First, the tax is taken off kitchen ranges. It should never have been put on. What is the first thing you need when you go into a house? You have to cook. Then commercial refrigerators, which is probably right. The government is so highly departmentalized that one minister does not know what another is doing. The Department of Agriculture has spent thousands of dollars to promote the saving of food through the preservation of foods by fast freezing, or freezing. The Department of Finance, on the other hand, was taking this machinery off the market so that farmers who had a surplus or people with gardens who had a surplus could not obtain fast freezers to save their foods.
One by one the taxes are being changed. The other day I noticed a bulletin containing items taken off the tax list, and the first thing I

noticed was commercial drink mixers. Now it will be cheaper to buy one of these than to hire a bartender. And, of course, to suit the ministers and some of the playboys, golf balls and clubs are taken off. But what is the second thing the veteran needs when he moves into a house after he has got his stove? An electric refrigerator. But there is twenty-five per cent on that.
The minister in the last debate said that an electric refrigerator was not really essential. I imagine he has one, though I do not suppose he needs one. If he put his food on the front porch it would freeze from the cold glances of people passing by. The Department of Health is a great department and I am glad I met them. Their Dr. Pett and nutrition and other pets have been going around the country at great cost to the taxpayer telling you how to refrigerate your baby's milk and how to save your leftovers. You can save $8.16 worth of food a month if you have an electric refrigerator. Of course, food is not a problem. The world is full of food. Who said that? At today's prices, the saving would be probably $10 or $15.
One lecturer said, "Save your calories- count 'em". As a matter of fact, he proved tc me that a banana split had more calories than a split banana. I did not get it. The second essential in a young veteran's home is an electric refrigerator, still subject to a twenty-five per cent tax-for what? To curry down this Canadian market, to destroy Canadian desire, to kill this Canadian purchasing power until the United States manufacturer can ship them in. There is no other reason. The government do not need money. They admit that, unless there is another election coming. I do not know.
Then they took the tax off pianos. I guess the minister likes jazz because he did not take the tax off organs. He does not like organ melodies, just hotcha. Why take it off pianos and not organs. There is less United States content in an organ than in a piano and I can prove it. In my riding we have two organ manufacturers and one piano manufacturer and I have compared the records. I find that there is a smaller percentage of United States content in an organ than in a piano. I am not speaking of pipe organs for churches. You have removed the tax from those; it should not have been put on. I am speaking about organs for cultural purposes, symphony orchestras and so on. Why take the tax off pianos and not off organs? I do not know whether the minister took the tax off bagpipes. I do not think they come under musical instruments.

Would it be some smart-aleck bureaucrat, or some legal man with a theoretical mind,-someone who knew nothing about business? We cannot tell. The ministry has the power; it does not matter who the man is. It is different in a company; you hire a man because he can do a certain thing. The way they move these ministers around you cannot tell who it might be. It might be myself; they have not offered me the job yet, but I am available.
Who can be judge of all things? What man in any party can be that? I do not think anyone can. Not long ago I visited the office where these permits are issued. They do not know what they are doing yet; they say, You fellows have not passed the regulations, so we cannot print our forms." They have them all pasted up with stickers, and if you change one you have to change the sticker, the fellow in London has not as yet even a blank on which to write. Do you know what they told me at that office? They said they might have 50,000 applications for import permits in ten days. Can anyone say that you can go into a huddle, produce a bunch of unemployed people, or people you draw from industry or from the legal or any other profession, herd them into a building, and expect them to know the essentiality of the thing you want to import? Could you expect them to pass judgment on what you want? Then I asked, "Who decides?" His reply was, "We decide." I asked if there was any appeal and his answer was, "No appeal. We decide."
Who are these smart people? I have been in business for twenty-five years, and I know I could not find a thousand people that quickly. I have fifty now, and there are only two or three smarter than I am. Who gets a permit and who does not? Well, you know there is an old saying in England, "He who has, gits." Perhaps that is it. Probably it will be the man best known to the person who has to decide; or it will be the firm that has the best approach or the best contact, or the firm that can put up the best brief or tell the best sales story. Little Joe Doaks up the alley, a hard-working businessman but no salesman, who cannot make a speech, who is shy when he gets to his feet-as I am-and who gets nervous, will not get a permit because he cannot put it over. I do not think they can find anyone who can be a judge of all things.
Let me give an instance in regard to these prohibited articles. I have all the respect for the minister who is to be in charge of this program. I think he did a grand job during the war. I do not question his ability as a businessman, but if he is right sixty per cent of the time he is better than most lawyers, because they only win fifty per cent of their cases. But let me give this instance. The minister, having supplied these thousands and thousands of houses that he dreams up in this chamber, has these regulations. What can you do in connection with housing? If you need soil pipe in order to get the roof on you can import it from the United States. You get the roof on and1 you get your first loan from the mortgage company, or the Central Mortgage Corporation. Then you have to have gyproc or plaster and get the walls up all round. What do you need next? According to the contractors, the next thing you must put in is the bathtub. That must go in so that the builder can finish up above it and around it. You cannot import bathtubs, and there are not enough available in Canada. They are banned absolutely; there are no permits issued. You can import carloads of vitreous china; you can import pedestal basins, fancy medicine cabinets, vitreous toilets and

all that sort of thing, but you cannot import bathtubs. That is the next item you need, but you cannot get it.
Incidentally, stoves are also banned. Of course many hon. members may say perhaps they should be, that we have a number of stove manufacturers in Canada who are doing a grand jo'b, and all credit to them. But one of their association tells me they cannot produce more than sixty per cent of the stoves that will be needed for new homes in the next two years. However, stoves are banned, so that people will have to eat hay or raw food.; they cannot cook.
I am sorry I did not hear the speech of the Minister of Trade andi Commerce (Mr. Howe) in Toronto today. I understand that, in connection with automobiles imported complete by dealers who have set up organizations in the last few years to buy cars made in the United States, they will be allowed a dollar figure of from $200 to $285 in United States exchange for every car they imported last year. They will be allowed this amount per car, regardless of the fact that they may bring in cheaper cars if they can get them. In other words, for every car a dealer imported during the basic period he will be allowed this amount of United States exchange. That is a pretty tough thing for a lot of these new dealers. In the first place, the franchise is automatically confiscated; and a franchise for any good car, in a good centre, is worth a good deal of money. His investment in his plant and showroom is very much depreciated, and of course, as a result of these two things, his bank credit is wiped out. Then, on automobiles made in Canada I understand they are going to give the manufacturers about $300 per car in United States exchange, to spend as they like. Further, I understand that the textile quotas are set at 32 per cent for the basic year ending in June, 1947, which is the average for the period from 1935 to 1939.
The trouble with all this program is that people in business do not know where they stand. They are frustrated. They cannot plan; they cannot design, and you cannot get firms from the United States to come over here. You cannot get risk capital. I talked to the head of a very large firm just outside Detroit, and incidentally I had influenced that firm to come to London instead of Peterborough, so that I am glad the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) is not here. I used to work with that gentleman years ago, and now he is financial director of one of the largest companies in that area. He decided he wanted [Mr. Manross.l
to open a plant in Canada, and as a matter of fact had already leased some property. But after his people had got in touch with our government he said the future was too uncertain. His whole excuse to me was, "You people change your minds so quickly we would not know whether we would be set for a year or two years." Incidentally, the twenty-five per cent excise tax was removed from one of their major products, and he could manufacture that if he could get a certain quota. He would employ from 250 to 300 people and would use 80,000 square feet of floor space, but there he is stymied. Now he says, "I think we will just wait and see."
That is a bad thing for Canada. You talk about monopolies or cartels; certainly this company does not belong to any such thing. That man worked with me about ten years ago, and he belongs to no cartel. He just built up something there; he has made some money; he has bank credit, and he said to me, " I do not care if we do not make money in Canada for seven or eight years. I do not care if we do not make a cent. We have a world-wide reputation. We are the largest builders of this product." I will not tell you what it is, because you would all be after this industry for your towns. He said, " We are the largest makers in the world of this article, and we make oil burners. If we did not make money for seven or eight years we would be quite happy. We would have an industry in Canada all ready to go. But we are stymied by this program." It would seem that I have driven the Minister of Finance out of the chamber; that is when a penny beats a dollar.
The two ministers are in a great predicament; they are having a pretty hard time of it It is not funny; they are in trouble. We can co-operate to help them out of their trouble- well, perhaps not to help " them," because I would not go that far. But I would go so far as to help Canada; and if we can help Canada and the Canadian economy, then we should do so.
These two ministers are the chief objects, the chief targets; I refer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Those are the two departments which will have to shoulder the burden of getting us out of the woods. One hears it said that the farther you run into the woods, the closer you are to being out. But it might be a big wood-and it is a hard wood, if you know what I mean. And that would not be funny, even if the other minister's name were Costello. A few of you got that one.
They will have to be magicians if they are to get us out of this in the few months mentioned in the optimistic forecasts of the

Minister of Trade and Commerce. As a matter of fact, they will have to be like Wood and Stone.
Have you heard the story about Wood and Stone? Well, Wood and Stone went down to the street corner. A pretty girl went past; Wood turned to Stone; Stone turned to Wood -and they both turned to rubber. It may be theory or magic or humbug-and I think it is the latter.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate this afternoon as I listened to it before the Christmas recess. The impression has been left that hon. members on this side of the house do not wish to take part in it. However, for a short time I should like to place before the house something of the history in connection with the devaluation of the Canadian dollar.
This afternoon Tory members have talked about the way in which the situation has been handled in the last few months. When criticisms are made by hon. members of the C.C.F. or Social Credit groups I feel that they are entitled to take the stand they may wish to take. This afternoon I have listened for some members in the Progressive Conservative party to tell us how a similar situation was handled when they were in power. That is something for which one would naturally listen. I was expecting that they would tell us how they handled a similar situation when they were in power.
I consider myself still a young man. Living on the border, I have seen a good deal of manipulation of United States and Canadian dollars. I believe it was in 1946 that I placed on record a brief history of the manner in which the United States dollar was handled at the time of the first great war, and this evening I should like to repeat part of what I said on that occasion, so that hon. members who were not here at that time may know the way in which business was then carried1 on.
In those days I was a comparatively young man and, as usual, was selling in the United States two-thirds of what I produced. When I received a cheque from a United States canner I would go to a Canadian bank. Then, as I said in the house before, if there were a few fish scales in my hair, or a little hayseed
around my neck I might perhaps get ben pel cent; but if I had a friend who knew the banker better than I did, he might get twenty per cent. There are hon. members on the other side of the house who can recall those conditions as well as I do.
When this war broke out in 1939 the government of the day decided that the exchange situation would be handled differently. During those days I could go to a bank and demand ten per cent for my United States dollar, just as could the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or any other hon. member who happens to sit on the opposite side of the house. All of us got ten per cent for our United States dollar.
Today the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said that if the Canadian dollar were devalued today the exporters of this country would reap the benefit of it. I have one little story to tell in that connection.
Mr. GREEN; On a point of order, I did not make any such statement. Indeed I did not deal with that subject at all. The hon. member must be confused.
This afternoon in his speech I understood the hon. member to say that if there were a premium on the United States dollar the Canadian exporter would receive the benefit of it.
No; the hon. member is referring to the wrong person.

That statement was made, at any rate, and I wish to explain it briefly. From 1930 to 1935 I was still an exporter in Charlotte. As usual under a Tory regime, the Canadian dollar was devalued. It went as low as from twenty to twenty-four per cent. At that time we were selling what we produced for about one-fifth of the amount we are getting today.
Then what happened? What I should like to know is: Have we any guarantee that the exporter would derive any benefit from that premium, if it did exist? United States can-ners from the state of Maine came across to the county in which I live. They exchanged their United States money for Canadian dollars and deposited it in Canadian banks. If I sold goods in the United States I was paid in Canadian dollars. Have we any guarantee today that if there were a premium on United States money the exporters of this country would derive the benefit from it?
In those days the county of Charlotte was represented by a Conservative, a very fine man( whom I know well. This matter was brought to his attention; it was a condition which existed for two or three years. The

American brought his United States cash to Canada and exchanged it for Canadian dollars, paying exporters in Canada in Canadian money. The same condition could exist today.
The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke about pushing the little man around. If he can think of any situation where the little man was pushed around any more than he was in those days, then I should like to have him explain it. I should like to hear some Progressive Conservative member in the house tell us how a similar situation was handled by his party.
The hon. member for Vancouver South also told us today about the manner in which trade pacts were made when the late Viscount Bennett was prime minister. I shall not argue with the hon. member; but I believe that the agreement with which this country has become connected within the last few months will be the greatest in Canadian history. After careful study I believe any hon. member would understand why it is the greatest trade agreement since confederation.
Another statement made was in connection with the diversion of Canadian trade to the United States. I believe if we are honest, and if we are familiar with the facts, we must all agree that the shortage of Canadian dollars was brought about to a great extent by the fact that we have shipped goods from this country overseas when they were needed overseas, goods which could have been sold in the United States for United States dollars.
As to the customs regulations, I think all will agree that these are the same regulations as have been in force for years and years. The only difference-and this is the complaint on the border where I live-is that in the last few months they have been enforced more rigidly. I agree that anyone living on the border will resent these regulations, but we hope that in the near future they will be changed.
I note that last week the press stated that the Canadian dollar was discounted in New York at less than eight per cent. If I remember correctly, when these regulations went into effect the discount was between twelve and thirteen per cent. Surely we must agree that they have brought about a change which is most beneficial to this country. I shall say no more about this matter, but I should like to hear one member of the opposition fell the members of this house whether his government handled a similar situation in any better way than this situation has been handled by the government in power at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with certain phases of the bill before us and call attention to the fact that the government have been very lax in dealing with this matter. They adopted a policy of drift and permitted matters to get into such a position that a real crisis has arisen at the present time. On May 6 of last year I was speaking on the budget and I said, as reported on page 2841 of Hansard:
I have watched with a great deal of concern the operations of the foreign exchange control board. I have felt certain over the past year, as I am today, that the operations of the board will work a great hardship on the people of Canada. It will mean that we shall have to take an immense loss which we would have been saved if the exchange had been allowed to find its own level. It is a sort of system of subsidies which people do not appreciate and which benefits most perhaps those who need it least, and in the long run the loss to the country will be considerable.
Then, referring to the excess of imports from the United States over exports I said:
If that continues, then surely as anything in this world Canada will lose a substantial amount of money by the operations of the foreign exchange control board and this will be another debt to be shouldered by the people of Canada.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the government must have known that every month since that time the foreign exchange control fund was being greatly depleted. One of the reasons why they were able to carry on as long as they did without public protest was the fact that they kept secret from the people of Canada everything which the people should have known. At that particular time we did not know the condition of the foreign exchange control fund. In fact it was nearly eight months after the facts were available to the foreign exchange control board before they were given to the public. I am certain that if the people of Canada had known during the fall and summer of 1947 the great extent to which these funds were being depleted and wasted there would have been such a public outcry that the government would have been forced to act.
Why did the government not act? Unfortunately they carried on their usual policy of drift, hoping that something would turn up. I do not know what they expected would turn up. They were away at conferences; they were trying to put through the Geneva trade agreements which they said would do wonders, but which at the very moment they signed them they knew they could not carry out. Unfortunately there were by-elections being

held in Canada at that time, and if ever there were an argument for refusing to allow a by-election to be held during the existence of a parliament, what happened during the late autumn presented it.
By-elections took place in Halifax and in York-Sunbury, and the government completely disregarded the people of Canada by making promises to those constituencies and withholding information the people should have had. We have only to remember the misleading statement sent out by the Minister of Finance as to the supposed surplus: "We had a surplus of $500 million; we had a surplus of $600 million; we were going on to have the greatest surplus ever known." The minister knew that any surplus which might have resulted from the revenues of the country was actually being wiped out through the losses of the foreign exchange control board and also by ignoring payments that were being made by the people of Canada in connection with loans where the money would not come back.
I should like to point out that for the first nine months of the present fiscal year ordinary receipts were only $1,925 million as compared with $1,894 million for the previous year. I wish to point out also that during December the receipts from income tax and excess profits tax were $50,000,000 less than last year. I know the Minister of Finance will say that this is not a true picture because receipts from income tax and excess profits tax vary greatly during the year and that payments on debts and other payments also vary greatly from month to month. I submit that it was only for the purpose of creating false confidence in the people of Canada that those statements of surpluses were made. The result is that the people of Canada have been spending money because they thought there was plenty of money in the country. The history of England shows that even with a great deal of domestic currency in the hands of the people, it does not mean anything. They simply have money to spend foolishly. They spend it at home on something that is no good to them, but they have no money to buy from foreign countries the things that they need.
This thing should never have been allowed to drift to its present condition. Steps should have been taken long ago. The people should have been told the things they are entitled to know. If the people had known that, there would have been such a public outcry, as I have said, that the government would have been bound to act. I remember last year the Minister of Finance-I think he was acting
minister then-said that this government was not run by experts, and then corrected himself by saying that the government was not run by the experts. Both statements are true. I have before me the proceedings of the Senate standing committee on banking and commerce held on August 20 and 21, 1946. Those proceedings were most interesting. I attended them and I can say definitely that, whilst the governor of the Bank of Canada estimated that during the succeeding six years the loss on exchange might be $600 million, he gave that only as an estimate. He gave that as an approximate amount. He went on to say that if there were any loss of confidence in Canada by the United States action must be taken to correct the matter. It was for the government to make the decision to have this foreign exchange control board. I think his blessing was most indefinite. It was the government's responsibility; the government knew what was happening and it did not act at the appropriate time. I should like to quote from page 42 of those proceedings where the minister was asked a question by Senator McGuire, to which he replied:
Hon. Mr. McGuire:	I should like to ask
Mr. Abbott a question. Now that exchange between Canada and the United States has been equalized, what is your intention with regard to Canadian currency, will it remain at par or close to par, or can you say what you would expect it to be?
Hon. Mr. Abbott:	That question, Senator, is
almost impossible for me to answer. Whether Canadian currency will stay at par with American currency or not will depend on so many factors, such as the uncertainty of the price level in United States compared with the price level here, that it is not possible for me to make any prediction. In view of the close relations between the two countries, I would hope that our currencies would stay at par. There is a great psychological advantage in their remaining in that position, but obviously if the Canadian dollar would buy considerably more in Canada than the American dollar would buy in the United States, it would not be possible to continue parity indefinitely; and the reverse would be true.
The Minister of Finance realized what could happen. He knew that he must act when the situation demanded action, and yet for reasons which it is hard for the people to understand he refrained from taking any action while our substance was being wasted every day, moneys which could never be recovered, and which should have been shown in his statement instead of a fictitious budget surplus being shown. I quote further from the evidence:

by direct action by your government?

Mr. Towers:	I think that is true. My suggestion was that if the situation was particularly difficult at that time there might be some public feeling as to whether or not the controls would be appealed.

My own thought is that if the circumstances were of the type we have been discussing, the action of parliament would be appropriate to the circumstances; but the public and business generally do not feel always absolutely certain until the thing is "fait accompli." I must add that in my remarks I was not speaking in the capacity of someone who was administering the mechanics of foreign exchange control but was rather thinking of the wider field of public uncertainty, should the thing come up at a time when the situation was particularly difficult.
Mr. Towers said before that committee that our imports from the United States in 1947 might go as high as $1,372 million. Actually we know they went up to $2 billion. Even today we do not know what the government plan to do to meet the situation. Their idea of meeting the situation appears to be to pass a certain bill containing a great many restrictions, all of which can at any time be abrogated or modified, and which will be administered by a minister who can say who shall be allowed to import and who shall not. No minister is in a position to do that intelligently with the knowledge he can get in the time available.
Sweden and Australia have gone about the matter in a very different way. Sweden has

deliberately balanced her exports with her imports so far as the United States dollar is concerned. Australia imported from the United States in the past year $133 million worth of goods and exported to that country $90 million. Australia said: We will balance our trade with the United States.
Why does this government not come before parliament with a definite policy for balancing our trade with the United States instead of going about the matter in this haphazard fashion? The government should be able to stand up and say what they will do and what they will not do. They have the figures before them. We know that in the twelve months ending August 31 last, which is the latest date I have figures for, although one month has since elapsed, we imported $85,000,000 worth of fruits from the United States; we can cut that down. We imported $24,000,000 worth of vegetables; we can cut that down. We imported $24,000,000 worth of nuts. Surely we can say that we will import only so many million dollars worth of nuts, and so on down the list. We imported $12,000,000 worth of coffee, $16,000,000 worth of tea, $13,500,000 worth of alcoholic beverages; $16,000,000 worth of unmanufactured wool and $17,000,000 worth of manufactured wool, $23,000,000 worth of paper. A statesman in Canada has said that we should not be importing this paper from the United States but that it should be manufactured in Canada. I do not think he got a great deal of credit from the Liberal newspapers for making that suggestion but was rather told that it threatened our good relations with the United States. Why should we not take steps to see that our pulp is manufactured in Canada and thereby save this $23,000,000 worth of imports?
We also imported $33,000,000 worth of books and printed matter. $63,000,000 worth of rolling mill products, $105 million worth of farm implements, $190 million worth of machineiy other than farm implements, and $147 million worth of automobiles and parts. I know the government have said that automobiles is one of the imports they are going to shut off, but they should be shut off on a percentage basis, and it should not be left to a minister to say: You can take this car and you can take that car.
We also imported $108 million worth of chemicals and $160 million worth of miscellaneous products. We can make a percentage cut in our imports of all these items. Surely this parliament of Canada, whose authority has been flouted a hundred times by this government, has a right to demand something more definite from -the government than it has disclosed so far as to its plans. Mr. Speaker, amongst the emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign excnange resources are certain prohibitions and restrictions regarding the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables. The effect of these prohibitions has already been seen in a shortage of supply of these essential fruits and vegetables, and the prices of those supplies which are available have already increased.
The first point where pressure is applied by any family which is in difficulties over its budget, in order that it may live within its income, is in cutting down its consumption of the choicest fruits which it purchases. If that is continued over an extended period the result will be that very shortly a vitamin deficiency will be noted and the health of the family will suffer on account of the lack of foodstuffs, particularly vegetables and fruits containing the essential vitamins. It seems to me rather ironic that, after the magnificent war effort which this country produced and the fact that certain fruits were subsidized during that period, being imported1 from the United States in order to maintain the health of the country, we should now be prepared to sacrifice nutrition as a means of balancing our budget.
I suggest that no economy, regardless of how well it may be balanced, can ever be worth the risk of lowering our national health. I suggest that there is a way in which these necessary fruits and vegetables can be made available to the Canadian people, because on the seaboard of British Columbia it is possible during the winter to raise all the vegetables and most of the fruits and berries which are mentioned in this table of prohibitions. For instance, we shall refer to the humble Brussels sprouts. Brussels sprouts grow out of doors the whole winter long on Vancouver island. You can go and pick the Brussels sprouts off their plants and they will provide vitamins which are necessary for the health of the veople. I know that people laugh at Brussels prouts and vitamins. There is an old saying of a greengrocer who was asked whether there were any vitamins in Brussels sprouts. He said', "No, ma'am, we have washed all these off". However, it is an established fact that even the humble Brussels sprouts are healthgiving vegetables. You can go through the whole lot that are included in schedule I and you will find that with a little care they can be produced by the horticulturists on Vancouver island.
When this list was first published a letter was sent out by the provincial department of agriculture urging the horticulturists of the Saanich peninsula to renew their efforts and to produce just this very type of winter vegetables which are now so urgently needed for the maintenance of the health of our people. I attended a meeting of farmers less than three weeks ago, and they were most anxious to meet the request as sent out by the provincial government. But they' asked a simple question, "How long are these prohibitions, restrictions, to be continued, because we shall have to make a considerable outlay if we are to bring under cultivation more of our acreage?"
In many parts of British Columbia the land is heavily wooded. Under the provincial scheme of land clearing, equipment is made available to the farmers, and country which a few years ago had been considered quite impractical to clear is now cleared with comparative rapidity by the use of the heavy machinery which is made available. It is amazing to see how the bull-dozers will go into thick forest country and uproot trees of considerable size, and then in a very few weeks' time than ground can be prepared for the growing of fruit, vegetables and berries, but of course that means a considerable outlay to the farmers themselves. Not only must they invest in a special kind of equipment, but horticulturists who are operating on a large scale no longer depend upon a man with a hoe to cultivate their fields; they have all kinds of power-driven farm equipment for the cultivation of their berry patches and their vegetables. If they can be assured that these prohibitions will be continued for some time they can meet the situation. But they are not prepared to make the outlay of capital which is necessary to clear additional land, to purchase additional equipment, unless they can be assured that by the time that new land is brought into production they will be able to be protected in the way they would be protected now if they had their vegetables to sell.
Also, not only is it a question of clearing land, but many of the fruits can be raised under greenhouse conditions. We are particularly fortunate in British Columbia regarding our greenhouse development, because our climate is more moderate than it is in other parts of Canada, and it is easy to heat these greenhouses to the required temperature and to keep them at a uniform temperature by the use of surplus wood and sawdust.. Sawdust is readily available from our many mills. Therefore it is essential that if the output of British Columbia fruit and vegetables produced in greenhouses is to be stimulated and

increased, there has to be a certain amount of outlay. I can refer to certain greenhouses on the islands in the gulf of Georgia which, before the last war, were operated by Japanese companies. These Japanese were removed during the war period, and to a very large extent their greenhouses have remained idle. Many of the panes of glass have been broken and the framework is deteriorating. A certain outlay would be necessary in order to bring these greenhouses back into operation;, but they could be brought back into operation very quickly, and they would be brought back if the minister would give some assurance as to the period of time that would be required.
I am not merely speaking from my own personal knowledge, but I know that representations have been made by the provincial government to the minister asking for an indication as to the length of time in which it might be considered practicable for these greenhouse people, the horticulturists, the fruit growers, to increase their production. I hope that before the minister closes this debate he will be able to give some indication that the production of these essential foods may be stimulated in British Columbia. I would ask him, if it is at all practical to make such a statement.
There is one other point to which I wish to refer and I do this in all seriousness, although it is possible that some hon. members may treat it somewhat lightheartedly. Two years ago I suggested in this chamber that in order to encourage the breeding of pure-bred race horses we should establish -a Canadian stud book so that a edit born and bred in this country might race on the tracks of Canada in those races which are specially reserved for Canadian-bred horses without having to register in the New York jockey club stud book. No action has been taken in that regard, although there is some talk that it was rather up to the racing associations of Canada.
I am not exaggerating when I say that in the last two years hundreds of thousands of Canadian dollars have gone in registration fees to the United States in order to register Canadian-born colts in the stud book of the New York jockey club. If it is necessary for us to restrict the number of Canadian dollars going over to the United States and to encourage United States dollars being paid into the Canadian treasury, why not adopt this Canadian stud book and make it essential that an entry fee be paid on all horses racing in Canada, so that if a Canadian colt born on the farms of Canada had to race on Canadian race trades all that would be necessary would be to register it in the

Canadian stud book, and if it were desired to race him on United States tracks, then of course he would have to be registered with the New York jockey club. Conversely, an American-bred colt anxious to race in Canada would have to pay an entry fee in order to race on Canadian tracks. That, I suggest, might be an avenue of exploration which might possibly interest the minister as a source of United States dollars coming into Canada and a means of drying up the stream of Canadian dollars being spent unnecessarily in the United States.
