I hope that the fact- that so many government members have remained silent throughout this important debate does not indicate that the people they represent in parliament are unaffected and undisturbed as a result of government policy. I think the administration is open to severe criticism for having failed to deal with the problem until December.
The minister, in introducing the legislation on December 16, outlined carefully that this problem was developing month by month. At page 326 of Hansard he said:
In the ten months up to October, Canada's imports from the United States have been running at the rate of nearly $2,000 million per annum, an increase of almost fifty per cent as compared with 1946 and four times as much as just before the war. In October, they reached the highest monthly figure on record of $190 million.
When we were here in July it was well known that the situation was developing and that some action should be taken. I am sure hon. members were not greatly impressed by the minister's statement on page 330 of Hansard:
I now come to an explanation of the import restrictions covered by the bill. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has emphasized, the government believed it unwise to impose any such restrictions before the Geneva agreements were concluded. At the same time, we could not postpone action until early in the new year when the new session of parliament would normally have met.
I cannot conceive that those who were participating in the formulation of the Geneva agreements could have offered any objection to Canada dealing with this problem last July or August or September; and if we had dealt with it at an earlier day we could have taken action that would have satisfied our 5849-371
people that fairer consideration was being given the matter. I happened to be in Prince Edward Island in November, shortly after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made his statement outlining the policy of the government. One of the fur producers of the island drew to my attention one of the publications of their co-operative association which complained about Canada's austerity program permitting the importation of raw furs from Russia, to be paid for with scarce United States dollars. I said, "I think there must be some mistake. I cannot conceive of Canada importing Russian furs and paying for them in United States dollars." On my return to Ottawa, however, I placed a question on the order paper and found that our importations of raw furs were increasing sharply, and that this had continued throughout the period. For the first eight months of 1947 we imported 87,950,000 worth of raw furs from the United States, as compared with $5,190,000 for the first eight months of 1946. For the first eight months of 1939 we imported from the United States raw furs to the value of $2,580,000, and for the first eight months of 1938 our imports amounted to 82,078,000.
While I have this table before me, I might mention that our imports of jewelry were still very high, $1,432,000 in 1947 as compared with 8417,000 in 1939. At the same time our importation of distilled liquors in the first eight months of 1947 amounted to $1,384,000, while in the first eight months of 1946 they, were $665,000, as compared with $49,000 in the first eight months of 1939 and $44,000 in the first eight months of 1938.
Coming back to the importation of furs from Russia, I find in the publication of the bureau of statistics, listing articles imported from each country for the nine months ending September, 1947, that we have been importing from Russia fur skins, raccoon, undressed; fur skins, viscacha, whatever that is, undressed; fur skins, fox, undressed; fur skins, Persian lamb, undressed; fur skins, rabbit; fur skins, squirrel. I think it would be difficult to defend, in the eyes of the Prince Edward Island fur producers who are having difficulty in meeting their obligations, the action of the government still considering it essential to import a luxury product such as raw furs from the United States, to sell in Canada in competition with the furs of our own producers. Nor can I think of any good argument why Canada should delay this long making a decision in connection with the importation of distilled liquors from the United States. Surely with our brewing and distilling capacity in Canada we should be able to produce enough to satisfy the appetite of all reasonable people.

It seems inexcusable to bar the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables, which have been regarded as a necessity by so many of our people, and continue the importation of raw furs, expensive jewelry and liquors.
While speaking earlier in the session, the minister had some comments to make regarding the point of view expressed by the leader of this group in referring to the discriminatory clauses which prohibited imports from the United Kingdom. The minister pointed out that the articles from the United Kingdom which have been barred do not represent a very large total, but I submit that a principle is involved. When manufacturers in Great Britain are trying so desperately to establish markets in Canada it seems an unkind blow for Canada to bar imports from that country which they were in a position to supply. For example, I find that we do not want any umbrellas ito be imported from the United Kingdom. That is not a very large item on the prairies, it is true, but I am sure my bon. friends from Vancouver and Halifax will consider that umbrellas have some place in our economy; and it seems inexcusable to bar umbrellas from the United Kingdom just because umbrella manufacturers in the United States say, " If you bar them from our country you must bar them from the United Kingdom." According to the report on imports for 1946, the United Kingdom was coming into that field to the extent of some $24,000, as compared with $116,000 from the United States. Then I come to fountain pens. The United Kingdom was commencing to export fountain pens; and I see no reason why we should bar fountain pens from the United Kingdom just because we happen to be short of United States dollars and consider it good policy to bar fountain pens coming from the United States.
Then I come to automobiles. I understand that some of the British automobile manufacturers had made extensive plans with a view to selling automobiles in the Canadian market.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are allowed in under quota.

In the year ending September, 1946, imports of United Kingdom automobiles to Canada had increased substantially over previous periods. Then the United Kingdom was coming into the Canadian market with sewing machines. I cannot see any good reason why we should bar these machines coming from the United Kingdom just because we want to close our doors to sewing machine manufacturers in the United States.

Then there are such items as paint, varnishes, shoe blacking, writing ink and a number of things included in the list of items being manufactured in Great Britain.
I want to support the opinion which has been expressed by various hon. members on this side of the house, that the legislation now before us cannot be interpreted in any other way than as an acceptance by Canada of even greater domination of our economy by the people of the United States, and a further blow to discourage the people of Great Britain in their attempts to rehabilitate their country. During the past few years I have been to the United States on several occasions; and while I must express appreciation of the warm hospitality I have been shown in the eastern, central and western United States, I must confess that everywhere I went I found that a very large number of the people in that country have queer impressions of Canada. They are of the opinion that we are a pretty backward people; that we are dominated by Westminster and that we are taxed heavily to maintain the monarchy in the United Kingdom. A great many are of the opinion that we drew very heavily on the lend-lease program of the United States. I was happy to be able to state everywhere I spoke in that country that, instead of drawing on the generosity of the people of the United States during the war years, we in Canada had a lend-lease program of our own, known as mutual aid, and that in terms of dollars per capita, as part of our contribution to achieve victory, we actually made larger contributions than did the United States through its lend-lease program. So I think the government of Canada should not allow Washington to influence it in this connection. At page 95 of Hansard for December 5, 1947, the minister said:
The United States in particular attaches great importance to the non-discrimination principle. While it possibly could not be called a fetish with them, it is a principle to which great importance it attached. The success of this emergency program and the smooth functioning of our economy depend upon the wholehearted cooperation of our friends to the south.
I cannot accept that view. I cannot think that any reasonable administration in Washington would not face up to our problem, and agree with us that since such a large percentage of our exports go to the United Kingdom, we must be permitted1 to set our own house in order and, certainly during 1948, to impart from the United Kingdom all- those commodities Great Britain is in a position to give us.	_
So far as the position in Great Britain is concerned, I think Canada should do some

bold and courageous thinking and acting at the present time. I happened to be in Europe twice during the period between the two great wars and travelled with a group of students in 1926, a large percentage of whom were from the United States. In France, Austria, Czechoslovakia-everywhere we went -we experienced bitter reaction to the United States. It was felt that they had used the war years to strengthen their own position, and that many of their wealthy people were going to Europe to buy up art treasurers and other rare commodities at low prices, taking advantage of the situation in which the people of Europe found themselves. It is a great pity that between world war I and world war II the United States failed to realize that the destiny of Europe affected vitally the destiny of the United1 States.
The United States came into world war I at a late stage; but, having entered it, she thereby, I believe, admitted that the outcome of the conflict was of vital concern to her people. Having made the decision, the United States would, I believe, have made a great contribution to civilization if, instead of finishing the war ini such a strong and rich position, she had used some of her reserves to help rehabilitate Europe.
I make the same statement with respect to world war II. If throughout the entire war the United States had sat on the side-lines and said that the conflict was of no consequence to her, we might not be too critical of the fact that they now find themselves in a strong position. But at one stage the United States did feel that the outcome was of vital concern to them and, having made that decision, all the resources of that country as well as those of Canada, the United- Kingdom and France should have been used for the common good, the cause of achieving victory.
The results of the war are still of vital concern to the people on this continent. I am proud of the fact Canada was able to make such a contribution; but I am not so happy when I think that during those war years apart from the men and women who actually joined the services, and the families of those who lost their loved ones, the great majority of Canadian people went through the war enjoying a higher standard of living than ever before in Canadian history. It was just our good fortune that our cities were not bombed and our homes destroyed. We did not have to go out on patrol night after night. Having shared in achieving victory, we should acknowledge the responsibility and see that those who lost their homes are assisted in rebuilding them, also that their industries should be re-established.
I have just received in my mail an interesting little booklet setting out some facts about Great Britain's economic position. I note that it was printed in the United States, and I hope it will have wide distribution and will be read by the people of that country. It points out that Great Britain's steel output of 12,900.000 tons in 1946 was twenty-two per cent above the 1938 figure. The production of trucks in Britain in the first eight months of 1947 was thirty-six per cent above the output in eight months of 1938. In 1947 the output in Britain of sulphuric acid, a key to the chemical industry in general, averaged thirty-three per cent above the 1938 level.
The booklet shows that cotton and woollen textile output is lower than pre-war in Britain, but the output of rayon and nylon yam is seventy-five per cent above pre-war. It states that before the war Britain produced only one-third of her food, but that through mechanization and intense cultivation she now produces one-half of the food consumed by her closely settled population.
If legislation of this kind is passed in Canada it will make it difficult for the people of Great Britain to continue to purchase Canadian agricultural produce. Not only will it affect the farmers on the prairies, the Maritimes and western Canada, but it will vitally affect every citizen in this country. It is a great misfortune that our administration has not brought in legislation which would give Britain a better break under present circumstances.
This same booklet gives some information respecting Britain's wartime losses, and some of the facts herein contained might well be brought to the attention of people in both Canada and the United States. It states that before the war half the cost of Britain's vast imports was covered by income from shipping and overseas investments, and only the remaining half had to be paid for by exports. Britain's shipping and investment losses during the war have thus created a heavy burden.
It states further that more than half of Britain's pre-war merchant shipping was sunk during the war. Even with new building and acquisitions Britain was left at the end of the war with 16,000,000 tons of merchant shipping, as compared with 22,000,000 tons before the war.
This booklet points out that, despite lend-lease, Britain had to sell overseas investments to a value of $4,500 million to help finance her war effort. In addition she acquired new indebtedness during the war amounting to SIX.500 million. This, together with losses of gold and dollar reserves brought her total wartime losses overseas to $17,000 million.

The booklet points out 'that, in addition to the loss of overseas income because of the war, Britain has had to meet new overseas responsibilities in helping to keep the peace and rebuild the world. British government expenditure abroad in 1946 amounted to $1,200 million, as compared with $64,000,000 in 1938. Britain has contributed more than $3,000 million in relief and rehabilitation abroad since the war. Whereas in 1938 British government expenditure abroad represented only two per cent of the country's total overseas payments, in 1946 it amounted to no less than eighteen per cent.
Then the booklet emphasizes something which is of vital importance to Canada when it points out that to meet the financial strain caused by wartime losses and post-war responsibilities overseas, Britain has to increase her exports to seventy-five per cent over the prewar level. Exports were cut back during the war to thirty per cent of 1938. A sixfold increase over 1945 is therefore needed.
How is Great Britain to be able to reach these objectives with Canada, for whom she is the best customer, treating her as we are treating her? In 1946 Britain received' a credit of $3,750 million from the United States and $1,250 million from Canada to help tide over the interim period of reconstruction-. The United States credit was used up more quickly than was expected, partly because of increased United' States prices, partly because of Britain's high dollar expenditure for Germany, but mainly because of the world's dollar hunger. Since the dollar countries are the main source of supply for so many goods, Britain had to use these dollars for essential purchases-or make them available to other countries-at a much faster rate than originally allowed for.
I think it should be recognized in both Canada and the United1 States that the treating of a starving Europe is a responsibility we cannot shirk. When they have imposed such strict rationing in the United Kingdom I suggest that we cannot behave as we are doing in passing legislation of this type.
In connection with the increased austerity in Great Britain, the booklet points out that almost all food is strictly rationed in Britain, including bread and' potatoes. The meat allowance per person has been cut from twenty-four to twenty cents worth a week; the bacon ration from two ounces to one ounce. The egg ration- is now about one a week. The non-priority milk ration is two pints per person a week.
All clothing is rationed in Britain. If a man buys one suit and an overcoat, he has

enough left of his yearly coupons to buy only two pairs of socks. If a woman buys a coat, a woollen diress, a pair of shoes and two pairs of stockings she will have left enough coupons to buy only one blouse.
I submit that we are unfair to a brave ally to expect that type of austerity program, while Canada delays month -after month to introduce the necessary changes to conserve our dollars and then is unwilling to take the people into its confidence and establish a broad basis for the barring of non-essential goods and the making sure that goods which are imported will be distributed- widely across the country and subjected to strict -price control, so that the Canadian manufacturer whose market is going to be ensured will be unable to take advantage of the short supply and prices not be permitted to skyrocket.
I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) speak this afternoon about the possibilities of the tourist trade in Canada. Some years ago, I made a computation which showed that the pavement put down during the war in our airports and military establishments was sufficient to -have provided an all-weather road from Halifax to Vancouver. I do not believe we could have got across to Victoria and Nanaimo, but we certainly could have crossed the mountains. That achievement was made possible when nearly a million of our men and women were in uniform and) three-quarters of a million in war industries, -at a time when there w-as a great- shortage of materials.
I submit that if between the beginning and end of the war Canada was able to construct, as a project for national defence and world security, runways and pavements to that extent we could -have, between .the end of the war and up to the present, assisted the provinces in building a Trans-Canada highway that would be a real attraction to tourists. When the state of Montana is able to get an annual grant of $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 from the federal government to spend- on its roads I see no reason why the provinces of Canada with their limited fields of taxation should not receive substantial grants from this government, so that as a peacetime measure we could build an all-weather road which would attract tourists to our country and send them from coast to coast in all kinds of weather and on a road that would be a pleasure to every motorist. If the government had embarked- on a project of that sort at the end of the war as a public responsibility I do not think we would have found ourselves in the critical position in which we are today.

In conclusion, I want to criticize the administration as severely as I can for failing to take action last year when parliament was in session. An announcement should have been made at the middle of the year that the then rate of spending could not continue. We should have cut down travel from this country. There is a complete bar to travel from Great Britain and I see no reason why we should not have cut down our allowances for travel as a temporary measure. A friend of mine went across to the United States for his holidays and he told me he was surprised to find that he and his wife could each get $500 without any question. The hon. member for Regina City pointed out that even the present limitation of $150 for every person in the country amounts to a very large total. If the government had acted last July and taken the people of the country into their confidence I think they would have had wholehearted support in the curtailment of the spending of short United States dollars for non-essentials. The people would have been willing to co-operate fully in carrying out any reasonable program.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke on the air on November 17 last he had a lot to say about the Geneva agreement. He said:
The new agreement contains a firm promise of real reciprocity in tariff reductions. It paves the way for full international co-operation in maintaining high levels of employment and expanding economic activity. It opens up to Canadian exports a larger and more equal access to the markets of the world than they have ever enjoyed. By virtue of these larger export opportunities, it will permit us, as a country, to concentrate our efforts on the production of those things that we best produce or manufacture, and so secure the highest level of real national prosperity.
At the very moment when the goal towards which we have worked over the years is at last coming in sight, we are unfortunately compelled to take a sharp detour over what I fear we shall find to be rough and difficult ground.
Apparently the detour the Prime Minister was talking about at that time was Bill No. 3, which we have before us tonight, respecting emergency measures for the conservation of Canadian foreign exchange resources. My first criticism of the bill is that whatever the government is going to do should have been done long ago. Just before the short session closed, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said that the government had expected that this business of shortage of United States dollars would level off. I would point out to the minister and the government that apparently they had their eyes on this matter during
the whole of 1947 but they did not see fit to act until November 17. That was too late because, as the minister tells us, by that time our United States dollars had run out until we had only some $500 million left.
I think a proper criticism that could be levelled at the government is that they let us down with respect to this dollar situation. The government could have explored and developed constructive measures for increasing our supply of United States dollars. If the production of gold should now be promoted in the interests of providing us with gold dollars or United States dollars, then it should have been promoted in the years before. It was only when we got .down to Noveroher 17 of last year that the government showed any intention of developing that industry in the interest of the dollar situation.
Both the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Finance have told us the effect of our buying so much steel from the United States, that that is one of the products which costs us so much in United States dollars. The fact is that the steel industry in Canada is expanding and we are getting to the point where we are almost self-sufficient. There are unlimited quantities of iron ore in Labrador and northern Quebec. If these resources had 'been developed, we possibly woidd have been saved from the emergency in respect of American dollars that we are faced with at the present time.
Coal is another commodity of which we have a goodly supply in Canada; but, for what reason I do not know, the government has never seen fit to develop our coal resources, and the consequence is that our money is flowing across the border in a continuous stream to purchase our coal requirements. I was in western Canada this fall and talked with the coal dealers in Alberta. They told me they can produce all the coal we need in eastern Canada, that all they want is to be assured of a continuity of markets. While the mines there are small, they are today producing all the coal that is required in western Canada and a considerable part of the coal requirements of eastern Canada. I think it is up to the federal government to do something about this great natural resource. If the mines require a large amount of modern machinery; if the whole plant has to be re-geared to produce coal in the quantities required, it is up to the government to do something along the line of a steady market. I am simply pointing that out, so far as the United States dollar shortage is

concerned, as one of many ways in which the government could have helped in the year 1947 to relieve the shortage of dollars.
Oil is another commodity of which we must have more than enough in this country to satisfy our needs, but we have not yet. done much to develop that industry. We know we have the oil resources, but so far the government has not paid much attention to their development.
Then there is the question of immigration. It may surprise the house to learn, as I did from a return, that 71,900 .people came in 1946 as immigrants to this country, as compared with a total population increase in the United States of 2,290,000. After all, our economy depends to a great extent on the number of people we have in this country. We are the third largest trading nation in the world and our future is dependent upon, our trade and commerce. Unless we look after immigration as well as conserving United States dollars we are being very short-sighted, as I think the government has been in regard to immigration. A Liberal member of parliament in Great Britain said the other day: "We have 50,000,000 people here and we have living space, employment and homes for only 40,000,000 people. So the logical thing would be for 10,000,000 of these people to find homes for themselves in different parts of the empire. That would be in the interests of themselves and of world economy." I believe that to be so. I believe that in that matter the government has been lax in developing the national economy in the interests of our country.
A poor job in public relations has been done in connection with Bill No. 3. The man on the street and industry in general do not understand it. I do not believe even the government understands it. I can speak with some feeling because I have been around different government departments trying to find out something about this bill. I ran into a very fine intelligent young man handling a certain branch of this work, but he knew just so much about it, and then sent me to another man to discuss matters further with him. From there I was sent to see the deputy minister of customs. But I first decided to go and see the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), and he said, "There is nothing to it. You do not have to see the deputy minister of customs." I found out in the end what the manufacturer wanted to know; but if I. a member of parliament, had to go through all that to get the answer to a simple question, how is the ordinary businessman to find out what he wants to know about this bill?
[Air. Timmins.]
I was glad that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) took time this afternoon to tell us something about the implications of this bill. I propose to cover some of the same ground myself.
There is an absolute prohibition in schedule I. None of the articles listed there can be imported at all unless, in the judgment of the minister, the prohibition is causing exceptional hardship. It turns out that a goo'd number of the items that were originally in schedule I have had to be taken out. Apparently the framers of the bill did not know as much about it as they thought they did. I know a firm in the city of Toronto engaged in the produce business which, in consequence of the restrictions imposed by this bill, has had to lay off four trucks and four of its employees. That is not good business to have employees running around looking for jobs as a consequence of government policy. As a matter of fact, I find that the Department of Labour of this government, in a review of 1947 labour conditions in the Dominion and prospects for the future, blamed the world's dollar-saving program with its import restrictions for putting more than a seasonal damper on the labour picture. The department in its review goes on to say:
Indications are this year that the decline in employment is slightly more than seasonal, since uncertainty as to the effect of import restrictions is dampening many employers' demand for labour, particularly in manufacturing industries.
My personal opinion makes little difference, but here we have a publication of the Department of Labour itself which says that this policy is bringing about unemployment to some extent, and we must pay attention to that.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has power of life and death over some of the industries concerned in schedule I. For those who have been engaged in the business of supplying these articles over a period of years these prohibitions are a serious matter. I saw hardwood flooring listed in the schedule at one time. I thought that was a wrong item to be in there, and apparently it was wrong, because not so long ago it was taken out of the schedule.
Schedule II is the quota schedule, and it runs to five pages having to do with textiles. Textiles is an important industry in this country. What is their quota under this schedule? It is cut down to thirty-two per cent of the amount marketed in the basic period. There are, no doubt, many dealing in textiles in this country who have made large commitments, perhaps have had textiles

designed to a particular order, perhaps had a certain stamp put on them for a certain customer, and now find they cannot fill these orders. Not only that, but the dealer has to tell the manufacturer in the United States that he cannot take the goods. He has broken the contract. First of all, he is liable in law for breaking the contract, but quite apart from that he has broken a connection which it has taken him years to build up. You do not stay in business unless you build up a connection over the years. He is in a position of frustration. He cannot buy the goods that he contracted for a long while ago. He cannot sell to the customer who is waiting for them. The customer is let down and cannot do with the goods what he wanted. But the position is even worse than that. The only other market he has in which to get these textiles is England, and they are not able to supply these goods. They cannot supply them for six months or perhaps for eight months. They do not even know yet whether they can get the goods or not. But if they can get them the price will probably be beyond that which the public in Canada can pay, because we know the cost of living is rising in England as it is here. Over there they have controls, but in spite of the controls the cost of living is rising beyond the control of the government, and we must not make any mistake about that. Further than that, they cannot produce the goods as cheaply in England as we can here; so that when the goods finally arrive here the purchaser has to pay a higher price than he intended to pay in the first place. Therefore he has to sell them to the consumer at a higher price. It does not take much imagination to see that again the cost of living has gone up. That is a concrete example in respect of a concrete industry, an industry that is supposed to be able to carry on at thirty-two per cent of its former level.
In so far as schedule III is concerned it has to do with the permit system. There again we have a minister, now the Minister of Trade andi Commerce, with life and death powers over the industry with respect to whether or not it can import the particular product. The first thing we have is intricate forms. Intricate forms are sent out to anybody who wishes to import into this country from the United States.
With respect to these materials, building stone and iron and steel which are prohibited at the present time, they can only be brought in under permit. I say that the government is in business. The government of Canada is in business today. It is in the business of running the country in a business sense. When you see a lot in a big city on which a building has
been torn down and the owners are prepared *to go ahead to erect a building on it, the plans are out; the contract is let; you find that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is also the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, says, I warn every industrialist; I warn any man who is thinking of putting up a commercial building at the present time not to do anything about it until he sees the department and gets the go-ahead signal in respect of the project.
Industrial construction is at a standstill. In the city of Toronto it is at a standstill. These projects cannot be gone ahead with and there will be unemployment in the industry very shortly. In addition to that, we were told by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in December that the restrictions in schedule III would go into force on February 1. Again there is more uncertainty. I read in the press that it is not coming into force on February 1 but will be postponed until some later day. Again we have uncertainty; again we find that the government is in business in Canada; it is doing the business of Canada. It is regulating people into bankruptcy. It may interest the house to know that bankruptcies in Canada are on the up-grade. In 1947 there were more bankruptcies than there were the year before.
I could name one or two industrial concerns which are engaged in the business of fabricating iron and1 steel products. If they cannot get the steel and, iron that they need they will certainly go into bankruptcy. The government is taking upon itself a very large load when it proceeds to deal with industry in this way. It may interest the house to know what some other people had to say about a bill such as this. We are objecting to the bill. In fact we are going to vote against it. It will be interesting to hear what the Prime Minister had to say about this sort of bill on April 19, 1934. He said:
When the government believes it is in the interests of its own policies it may pass any order it pleases with regard to the trade of Canada, regardless of the legislation parliament itself has enacted or may enact. Do hon. members (of the Commons) realize that this bill gives to the (cabinet) the power to prohibit absolutely the importation of goods from another country which the government may allege it is in the public interest to prohibit? Do bon. members realize that it gives the government not only the power to prohibit imports, but the power to prohibit exports of goods from this country? This parliament is to part altogether with its right to say what is to be imported or exported. As I have said the effort is to get away from parliament altogether.
I was not in the house in 1946 when the Foreign Exchange Control Act was passed, but I read what the Minister of Finance

had to say. He said that the regulations of the foreign exchange control board were not passed for the purpose of dealing with a matter such as this, but our law officers have told us that wb could do so; so we have decided to do it, in November, 1947, and all we ask you men of parliament is to come here and be a rubber stamp for us in respect of this resolution, because that is all it amounts to. You brought us here in December and gave us a couple of days to deal with the matter; you have now brought it down again, and we are to have a couple of days to deal with it now and another couple of days probably a little later on. But, after all, you expect us to pass this bill. You have made it law. You have told the people of Canada what they have to do in respect of these matters. It is like trying to make a river run backwards. The government is saying to the United States companies, "we want your branch companies in Canada to do more manufacturing in Canada, to manufacture goods in Canada to sell back in the United States in competition with your own goods over there." It just does not make sense. I have known of a lot of United States concerns which have come to Canada. I must say that their financial record in the last ten or fifteen years has not been very good in dollars and cents. They have not sent very many dollars back to the United States. I do not think for a moment they are going to take their cue from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not think they are going to venture into paths of which they know nothing with the hope that they will make money, and, in addition, compete against their own parent companies in the United States.
I thought the house would be interested to hear of a little article that appeared in the Times-Review of Fort Erie under date of November 27, 1947. It reads as follows:
By now, anyone who has a radio or reads a newspaper knows what the government did. It announced the most ill-conceived, unintelligent plan it has ever devised for the correction of our imbalance of trade with the United States. While still maintaining the fiction that a Canadian dollar is worth an American dollar, the plan involves prohibition on the import of an extensive list of commodities; greater restrictions on the transfer of money across the border; new excise taxes, and whatnot. All of which means the employment of more civil servants, enforcement officers and, above all, bureaucrats. Already the effects of this program have made necessary the reimposiition of price ceilings on most canned fruits and vegetables.
I think that epitomizes in the minds of the people the result of the program. Next we

have a quotation from Saturday Night of December last, which reads:
How long will this government direction of business continue? Mr. Howe suggests it may be only a few months.
Well, we know what "months" means in the language of the minister. It means years, because in the course of questioning in the house in December last he admitted that months did not mean nine or ten or eleven months but might mean years. So we know where we stand in this regard. Go into any department and they will tell you that it means, as a matter of fact, from eighteen months to two years. The quotation continues:
Actually the government will only be getting its controls into working order (if it is lucky) by that time. If the controls are not going well, the tendency then will not be to relinquish them but to intensify them.
Is there anything surer than that?
This has been the experience to date in England. When national socialism has failed to deliver the results hoped for, the procedure has always been to increase the dose.
Not only are we in trouble in respect of this one bill, but the government is in trouble in respect of a good many other things as a result of being in business. The government has been in business in connection with the wheat agreement, and the farmers of Canada are not satisfied with the treatment they have received through government business under the wheat agreement. The government gummed up the coarse grain situation by withdrawing the subsidy. They are in business in respect of coarse grains too. In the matter of the trade agreements with Great Britain they managed to get iprices raised on some commodities, and the result has been that the price to the consumer in Canada is raised also. They are in the business of bacon as well, and the price of bacon has gone up. These measures are all combining to increase the cost of living in Canada and the government must accept its responsibility in that respect.
Furthermore, we are being drawn into the United States orbit year by year. I can remember as an undergraduate at college hearing the late President Taft making an address in Toronto University. He said that somebody had asked him whether he did not think the United States would like to take over and govern Canada. He said, "Speaking for myself as President of the United States, all I want to say is that I have enough trouble of my own". That may have been President Taft's attitude in those days, but

Foreign Exchange Conservation
the situation is developing to the point where we are not going to be a partner of the United States but a poor relative, and very soon too. With 12,500,000 people here and 142,000,000 over there, it will not be very long, unless we do something about immigration, before we are swallowed up. Immigration has much more to do with the economy of Canada than this policy which we have before us tonight.
The procedure that has been adopted in respect of this bill seems to be pretty much a hit-or-miss one. The other day, dealing with the matter, the minister said, "If we do not like one method of dealing with these problems we will find another." That is not the way a businessman runs his business. He is responsible to his board of directors and, after all, we are the board of directors of Canada. Hon. members sitting on the other side and we on this side are all responsible, and now we are dealing with a measure which will turn everything topsy-turvy-everything that we have done up to this time in Canada. The government is asking businessmen to get out of one kind of business and into another. How can it be done? How can the government expect a firm that has accumulated knowledge with regard to one category to deal with something quite different? It is quite impossible.
I say, therefore, that the task of the government, much as we would like it to succeed, is impossible. We are going to be back to the point where they will have to put on more restrictions and controls in order to try to make the thing work. When the former minister of veterans affairs said that he was to a great extent in favour of socialism, he
was, I believe, speaking his mind, and there are many members on the other side who, I believe, are also thinking in terms of socialism, particularly in connection with this measure which they are asking us to put through.
If this is to be foisted on us, particularly schedule III, instead of one man being the Pooh-Bah in the cabinet and in the house, there should be a board something like the national selective service board, with a group of businessmen sitting in with the minister to deal with these matters of discretion.
I sat down in Toronto some weeks ago with a certain man and we went over a certain section in schedule III. I said to him, "What do you make of that?" He replied, "As a matter of fact, I drew that section for the department of customs three or four years ago. I know every single word in that section and I know what it means, but I doubt whether there is a man in the department who knows it as I do." I believe he was speaking the truth. I feel certain that most of the items in this schedule III are better known to businessmen than to any man in the department, and I see no reason why things of this kind should be left to the life and death power of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
On motion of Mr. Timmins the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall continue the discussion of the measure we have been considering today.
